Interesting. I know very little about this topic, but as I read my thoughts immediately went to the evolutionary biologist Robert Sapolsky and his book The Trouble With Testosterone. I would encourage you to go down that pathway and add it into your thinking. I’m curious what the Bolt people would say to these arguments.

It has been some time since I read the book so I got some LLM summaries to refresh me on why many evolutionary biologist consider testosterone an expensive biological tax. I’m going to paste some of it here:

In the wild, maintaining high testosterone levels is akin to driving a car with the engine red-lining. It provides short-term power for mating and fighting, but it wears down the machinery (the body) much faster. Here is a breakdown of the specific evolutionary costs Sapolsky and other biologists highlight, focusing on the immune system and metabolic “taxes.” 1. The Immunocompetence Handicap This is the central theory explaining why high testosterone is costly. The “Handicap Principle” suggests that because testosterone suppresses the immune system, only males with superior genetics can afford to maintain high levels of it. The Trade-off: Energy is finite. The body must choose between investing in survival (immunity, cell repair) or reproduction (muscle mass, aggression, mating displays). Testosterone forces the body to prioritize reproduction at the expense of survival. The “Honest Signal”: High T features (like a peacock’s tail or a stag’s massive muscles) are “honest signals” to females because they are dangerous to possess. The male is essentially saying, “Look at how strong my genes are—I can handicap my own immune system with this much testosterone and still be standing.” Parasitic Load: In wild primate studies, males with the highest testosterone often have the highest burden of intestinal parasites. Their immune systems are less efficient at fighting off low-level infections because their energy is diverted elsewhere. 2. Metabolic & Physiological Costs Beyond just the immune system, high testosterone extracts a heavy toll on the body’s daily maintenance. Metabolic Burn: Testosterone is metabolically expensive. It forces the body to build and maintain lean muscle mass which burns calories at a much higher rate than fat. In a food-scarce environment (which is most of evolutionary history), having high T is a risk; you are more likely to starve during a famine. The “Good Cholesterol” Crash: Testosterone generally lowers HDL (good cholesterol). Sapolsky notes that this is one reason why males across many species die younger than females. The hormone that helps you win the fight today clogs your arteries for tomorrow. 3. Behavioral “Taxes” High testosterone lowers the threshold for risk-taking, which carries a direct survival cost. Injury and Mortality: High-T males are more conspicuous and more likely to engage in risky confrontations. In the wild, “winning” a fight often leaves a victor injured, making them susceptible to infection (which their T-suppressed immune system is now less equipped to fight). Parental Investment: Evolutionarily, there is often an inverse relationship between testosterone and parental care. High T drives mating effort (seeking new partners) rather than parenting effort (caring for offspring). In species where offspring need high investment, high T can actually be an evolutionary disadvantage if the offspring die from neglect. Summary of the Trap The “trouble” Sapolsky identifies is that while high testosterone might help a male pass on genes (by winning a mate), it actively works against his staying alive. The Irony: Pro-TRT (Testosterone Replacement Therapy) arguments often frame high T as the key to “health” and “vitality.” From an evolutionary standpoint, nature views high T as the exact opposite: a calculated health risk taken solely to reproduce before you die.

I hope this is good food for thought and discussion. Thanks for your years of great blogging MMM!

Did you do any research on dosing daily versus once or twice a week? My concierge physician has me on twice per week and I’m curious about how it might affect me if I switched that to a daily smaller dose. Any insights you have?

Testosterone cypionate (most common, what MMM is using) and enanthate (another commonly used ester) have a half-life of around 10 days, meaning that 10 days after your dose about half of it will be left. After a few weeks of weekly dosing the levels stabilize (you can math this out using mg if you want). There’s zero reason to dose daily. I actually tested twice-weekly dosing vs weekly with blood testing and there was no difference in my levels. Weekly is more than fine and you won’t notice any fluctuations. It’s pretty common for people to dose every other week, but weekly is more than sufficient to maintain consistent levels.

#8455. Pain And Penalty: Why A Dad Bod Challenge Works When Willpower Doesn’t

If you want to lose weight and gain muscle, join a dad bod or a mom bod challenge. The social pressure to hit your goals will be immense. And if you put a financial penalty for not meeting your goals by a certain date, you will be even more motivated to get fitter.

Since graduating from college in 1999, I've weighed between 164 and 173 pounds at 5'10” tall. I'm currently about 165 pounds, 45 days after the start of my Dad Bod Challenge. The lightest I weighed as an adult was about 153 pounds, which lasted all of one year before I gained the freshman 10+ pounds during college.

After college, my doctor also suggested I should be around 155-157 lbs to hit my ideal weight. So for over 25 years I've been telling myself I'd like to lose 10 pounds. And I've never succeeded, only coming close when I grew to 173 pounds during the first year of fatherhood in 2017, and then again during the first year of COVID. After both periods, I ended up losing about 7 pounds at most.

But after hearing about some fellow dads at my kids' school entering the Dad Bod Challenge and losing a ton of weight while also gaining muscle, I was impressed. This could finally be the impetus I was looking for to lose that stubborn 10 pounds!

Let me explain our setup, so you might be incentivized to create your own. After all, once you're financially on track, you should get physically on track as well.

There are actually 10 of us in the Dad Bod Challenge. Here are the conditions:

$5,000 might sound steep, or to some, it might not sound like much. But overall, the penalty needs to feel painful enough to motivate you to lift weights, exercise, and reduce food consumption. A $1,000 penalty would be enough to get me motivated, while another might need a $50,000 penalty.

$50,000 would be a scary number to lose, especially as cash strapped as I am. However, on the flip side, with such a high penalty, there is no way I wouldn't meet my goals.

Overall, we agreed that $5,000 was a high enough penalty. After about 45 days, the judge also offered dads the option to buy an extension for $500 a week, for up to four weeks. If a dad buys the extension and meets his objectives, he gets all his money back and doesn't have to pay the $5,000 penalty.

This lifeline was a great relief for me given my slower-than-expected progress. But I'm also reluctant to take it because I need PAIN AND PENALTY to keep me motivated.

If you think losing weight is hard, try losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time. Way harder.

Muscle needs protein and calories to grow. A calorie deficit, which is how you lose fat, starves your muscles of the fuel they need. So the two goals fight each other.

Losing weight on its own is relatively simple. Track what you eat and run a daily calorie deficit large enough to hit your fat-loss target by a certain date. You don’t have to do more. You just have to eat less. Exercise helps, but roughly 80% of weight loss comes from diet. And if you exercise too much, you might overeat.

Building lean mass, which is mostly muscle, requires lifting weights. And not casual lifting. You need to lift to failure, where you can’t squeeze out another rep or two. That usually means at least three sets of 8 to 12 reps, adding weight over time to discover what you can really do.

When I was young, piling on more plates was a fun challenge. Now my joints and tendons ache when I push to the max, and that’s when the injury risk spikes.

Fellow dads have torn biceps, triceps, and pecs, and thrown out their backs lifting. My 70-year-old uncle, who looks like He-Man, tore a shoulder muscle this year and needed surgery. He’s out for at least two months.

If I get seriously injured, I will most likely fail the dad bod challenge. To win, or at least not lose, every dad must hit both his fat-loss and lean-mass goals at the final scan concurrently. You can’t hit your muscle target two months in and then lose it during the final 45 days because you focused only on cutting.

Body recomposition is far harder than doing either one alone. And this is my first time doing it

I hadn’t regularly lifted weights in over 10 years before this challenge.

The reasons were mostly laziness and boredom. I also have a shoulder injury that’s nagged me for at least six years. During COVID, I couldn’t throw a softball overhand without pain, so I mostly played first base and occasionally third. I’d rather not have surgery.

My hope was that going from zero to one would produce big gains. But I needed to be careful. If I hurt myself further, I might not be able to lift at all.

For 45 days, I watched what I ate. I cut way back on sugar and carbs and loaded up on protein shakes and chicken. On top of playing tennis and pickleball three times a week for about 1.5 hours a session, I added 30 to 40 minutes of walking a day.

After all that, my DEXA scan showed I’d lost only 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean tissue. I expected at least 4 pounds of fat loss, so I was disappointed. But I’m pleased with the lean tissue gain.

The good news is I still have about two months to go.

Over the next two months, I need to gain another 1 pound of lean mass and lose 11 pounds of fat. That’s a net loss of 10 pounds, which would put me at about 156.5 pounds. But a DEXA scan can easily fluctuate by half a pound, so my safer target is 156 or less.

I haven’t been under 160 pounds in 26 years, but I’ve dreamed about it, just like how I've dreamt of buying a mansion in paradise. Then reality sets in and bludgeons my hopes into the ground.

Kei Nishikori, a pro tennis player I’ve followed, has played at around 155 pounds at 5'10”. If he can do it, so can I. Of course, he’s a professional athlete who works out five hours a day and I’m a 49-year-old dad who writes. Still, I accepted the challenge.

As a tennis and pickleball player, I want to be lean. Big muscles are nice, but they slow down my speed and hands. It’s one reason you don’t see muscular players on the pro tour. To each their own.

The best part of a Dad Bod Challenge is the group. Everybody is supportive and brings a different nutrition and fitness background. We cheer each other on and answer each other’s questions. Although, some remain completely silent.

I don’t think anybody is primarily motivated by winning the other dads’ money. Everybody seems motivated by the chance to improve their health.

What’s interesting is that the goals aren’t uniform. We entered knowing the penalty and our own targets, but once the challenge started, we could see everyone else’s.

The judges tried to set fair goals and meet each dad where he was. But after seeing all the numbers, I probably should have negotiated a smaller fat-loss target.

For example, my buddy is two inches shorter than me and started 38 pounds heavier. He has to get down to about 196 pounds while I have to get down to 156 pounds. Our body compositions are different, as he has more lean mass, but losing a similar percentage of fat when you have less of it is harder.

That's life. Which brings me to the lessons a Dad Bod Challenge teaches about money and life.

Getting ripped and wealthy doesn't just happen. You've got to make it happen. Nobody is coming to save you.

The only reason I exercise is because tennis, pickleball, and softball are fun. If they weren’t, I wouldn’t. I don’t run for fun. I don’t walk for fun, although I do enjoy a nice hike.

This lack of fun is the main reason I stopped lifting weights. If I’m going to lift something heavy, I want to be productive, like hauling rocks and bags of mulch for a landscaping project. Curling a dumbbell in a gym felt pointless.

A Dad Bod Challenge forces discipline when fun isn’t enough. It gets you out the door for a 6 am run before work, or to the gym at 9 pm once the kids are in bed. The challenge also helps you get used to that throbbing feeling of hunger, which may make you more appreciative of the things you have.

Make the challenge long enough, 100 to 180 days, and the discipline compounds until it becomes part of your weekly routine.

Building wealth requires the same consistency. You need the discipline to save as much of each paycheck as possible, and the courage to put those savings at risk. Historically, stocks have gone up in roughly 70% of years. That’s when you feel great about your efforts, like losing fat and gaining muscle. The other 30% of the time, you lose a little or a lot and curse your timing, like getting injured.

Stick with both routines for 10 years and you’ll be blown away by the results. But staying disciplined for that long is hard. That’s where a workout buddy more gung-ho than you helps. It’s also where an automatic 401(k) contribution from every paycheck and an AI investment advisor helps.

Some people are born to wealthy, loving parents. Others are born into poverty, given up for adoption, or lose their parents as babies. Some people befriend the founders of a hot AI company and join before it hits it big. Others join startup after startup that goes bust.

The body is similar. Some people are born with fast metabolisms and uncanny strength. Others pack on weight despite working out constantly. Tall, skinny people may struggle to add muscle. Shorter, stockier people may bulk up with ease.

At 49, I'm one of the oldest dads in the group. The youngest is 39. Ah, I remember 39. I was five years into FIRE, traveling the world, and recovering much faster than I do now. I also didn’t have my shoulder and knee injuries. But the challenge gives older dads no handicap. No easier fat-loss targets, no lower lean-mass goals, no extra free time.

Compare your goals to someone else’s and you might get annoyed, because you have completely different genetics. The judges try to set fair goals, but they won’t get it perfect every time.

We can’t control the hand we’re dealt. We can only control our effort and attitude. So compare your progress to your old self and nobody else. If you hit your own goals, you won’t lose. If you happen to win some money too, great. The money was never the point.

What I love about my Dad Bod Challenge is that the creators and judges are fitness fanatics. They’re smart, enthusiastic, kind, and extremely fit. They’ve experienced the benefits of being in shape, so they’re paying it forward by organizing a challenge for 10 dads who are nowhere near as fit.

I’ve learned a ton about how to train, what to eat, how to recover, and how to supplement with protein. One example: spread your protein out, eating about 20 to 25 grams every few hours instead of cramming it all into one meal for better utilization.

Oh, and did you know a tablespoon of olive oil is around 120-140 calories?! Nuts!

I also lost all my excuses. I used to tell myself only people without kids or demanding jobs could get extremely fit. But the judges are dads and successful entrepreneurs. Excuses gone.

Paying it forward is also why I’ve published three times a week on Financial Samurai for over 17 years. No courses, no paywalls, just free content based on my experiences to help you reach financial freedom sooner. When I find a great strategy, like negotiating a severance if you plan on quitting anyway, I find it impossible not to share it.

Before this challenge, I had never measured my lean mass. I just stepped on a scale. But a scale lies by omission. You could lose two pounds of muscle and think you’re making progress. That's no good, especially for folks over 40 who begin to lose muscle more rapidly.

The DEXA scan showed me the truth. After 45 days, I’d lost 2.6 pounds of fat and gained 1.4 pounds of lean body mass. The scale only showed a 1.2-pound difference, which would have been demoralizing. The DEXA showed real recomposition, but also still a bummer because I thought I would have made greater gains.

Finances work the same way. Plenty of people only look at their income or checking account balance and think they’re doing fine. But income is just the scale. Net worth is the DEXA scan. It shows whether you’re building assets or just shuffling money around while debt quietly piles up.

I’ve tracked my net worth since 1999 and it’s one of the best financial habits I’ve ever built. Whatever you measure regularly, you naturally start to improve.

Empower is what I use to track my net worth once I moved on from spreadsheets in 2012. Mezzi is what I use to track my public investments and gain powerful financial insights to better optimize my portfolio.

At the end of the day, I want to build muscle and lose fat to increase my chances of living a longer, healthier life.

That’s primarily why I think more people should join a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you miss your exact targets, you’ll likely finish in better shape than when you started.

In high school and college, I stayed in shape to have the widest dating pool possible. My four years at William & Mary were a blast.

Once I started working, good dieting and regular exercise went out the window. During my first five years, staying under 170 pounds was a struggle. Eventually I settled into the mid-160s, playing competitive USTA tennis for 10 years and wanting every edge I could get.

Now, I want as much energy as possible to play with my kids. And I want to live long enough to meet my grandchildren.

So if you need a reason to get in shape and change your body composition, organize a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge. Even if you lose, you’ll probably make new friends and end up fitter.

Here’s to greater strength and 156 pounds or less by December 23, 2026. More importantly, here’s to a lifetime of healthier habits going forward.

Readers, have you ever joined a Dad Bod or Mom Bod Challenge with real money on the line? How big does a financial penalty need to be before it actually changes your behavior, $500, $5,000, or $50,000?

Life insurers notice when you get in shape. Your weight and health history help determine your health class, which drives your premiums. I had my first child two months before turning 40, so my kids will depend on me well into my 60s. Term life insurance is the cheapest way to make sure they’re OK if I don’t make it to grandparent duty.

If you have dependents, check out Policygenius. You can compare quotes from multiple top insurers in one place instead of calling around. The best time to lock in a policy is while you’re young and healthy. The second best time is right after you finish a Dad Bod Challenge. Both my wife and I got matching 20-year term life insurance policies with Policygenius and we feel mentally great as a result.

I probably would have recommended the first 45 days of lean bulking (eating 200 calories more than you needed) to reach your muscle goals in the first half of the challenge, then to spend the remaining time preserving that muscle through exercise but losing all the fat though an extreme cut (including the extra 2.5 lbs of fat from lean bulking).

Yeah, it’s gonna be a really difficult challenge. My head is spinning on how the heck am. I’m supposed to lose another 10 to 11 pounds of fat while gaining another 1 pound of lean body mass.

My fear is that I cut aggressively and then I just end up losing lean body mass too, which would result in a failure of my challenge. Measuring the weight is easy as I can just step on the scale, but measuring the lean body mass is hard.

I have until December 23, so I have over 60 days, not 45 days.

Then I can buy four weeks of extension at $500 a week. If I hit both goals, then I don’t have to pay the extension fee and $5,000 penalty.

That’s good you have extra time. Yeah, I think aim for gaining the muscle first, then once you confirm you have it, switch to cutting, and use your extensions to get the rest of the fat off. Last year I lost 60 lbs in 4 months. Admittedly at least 7 lbs of that was muscle. Creatine helps muscle gain a lot, so I would use it for the next 30 days.

Wow, 60 pounds is a lot! Congrats. I will be 107 pounds if I lost 60 pounds, which is impossible.

How tall are you and what was your starting weight before you lost 60 pounds?

I have to lose the same amount of fat as a fellow dad who is 2 inches shorter than me, but weighs 205 pounds starting versus my 167 pounds starting. So it’s a pretty tough challenge.

Thank you! I rebounded a bit but mostly still fit. I am 6-5” and starting weight was 265 lbs. I dieted down to 209 lbs, then got sick and was 204.8 lbs for one day lol. Now I am back up to 222lbs or so. Age 34. You got this Sam!

As a physician, there are GLPs, peptides, and testosterone that make any competition less than equal (fair), so if you don’t win, presume they cheated! lol

Nah, our contract says no weight loss drugs. But I have thought about it and once I did research, I realize these drugs just make you not want to eat, right? It doesn’t actually do anything to burn fat or build muscle.

So if that’s the case, I’d rather not take a pill or inject myself since I know how to just not eat. But maybe I’m missing something?

GLPs have a big impact on how your body processes food. It’s not just “not being hungry”. For example, back when I was a 40 year old woman, I weighed 145 lbs (I’m 5’7″) and was “pre diabetic”. 15 years later after a year of a low dose of Zepbound, I’m 165 lbs with a normal A1C. I’ll take that over a lower weight any day. I have a strong family history of diabetes, so I’m more interested in addressing it rather than purely focusing on my weight. I also want to keep as much muscle mass as I can as I get older. I didn’t do a DEXA scan before taking the shot, but am thinking about it now. I walk 1.5 miles 6 days a week, lift weights 3 times a week, do yoga 2 times a week. If I weighed what the tables above said, I’d be ill. At 145, I looked like I was sick.

If you have Netflix, watch Game Changers. It’s excellent and will give you a great perspective about gaining muscle whilst keeping excess fat off.

Oh wow that’s intense! Props to you for taking on such an incredible challenge that is focused on improving health. I never thought about the complexity of losing fat while gaining muscle. So much of society’s focus is on losing weight and rarely on gaining muscle let alone losing fat AND gaining muscle. Glad you’ve been learning a lot in the process and are improving your fitness. Way to go!

Try carnivore entirely, or at least no carbs from 5pm to noon every day. Read the studies how frequent carb snacking and eating carbs at night keep insulin elevated all the time, which inhibits the breakdown of stored fat (lipolysys). Start your day every day for the second half of your challenge with multiple eggs, bacon, and steak. Stop all seed oils. Get rid of your protein shakes. Go ahead and eat real virgin Olive oil. Do fasted workouts in morning.

Do you know your height, fat percentage, lean body mass, and overall weight? I just finished change for you as you aged? How old are you?

I would be cautious about following blanket carnivore advice. You want to do it the right way. While carnivore is inherently low carb and therefore helps the insulin levels stay low and can help lose weight, it can absolutely skyrocket your apob / LDL because of the amount of saturated fat which in turn increase cardiovascular risk (particularly in asians). A balanced mediterranean diet has the most evidence and likely the most compliance long term. But if you decide to do a more drastic diet, please check your labs pre, during, and post diet to ensure there are no concerns.

As a physician, I see patients struggle all the time and diet is quite individualized, so there’s no one size fits all. Anyway, I’m happy you’re doing this challenge! Fitness and health are incredibly important. I try to stay around 150–155 lbs, although I tend to lose muscle quickly if I’m not consciously eating enough protein or if I’m playing too much tennis and not lifting enough. In my mid-30s with two kids under two, it’s getting harder to balance everything. I do DEXAs every 1–2 years and just found out my body fat went from 13% to 15% without any increase in lean mass. Still healthy, but not the direction I’d like to be heading. As long as I can maintain my strength and tennis level, I can live with it. Still USTA 5.0 for now, with the goal of maintaining that singles level through 40 or even 45!

Also, as a shameless plug, I have a substack called PREHAB that you can check out and may find interesting…I write about healthy aging, things like resistance training, full body imaging, creatine supplementation, protein, saunas, cold plunges, cholesterol, etc. Your story and writing actually helped inspire me to start writing on the side, although I definitely don’t have your dedication to publishing so frequently. It’s hard work!

5.0 is great! And tough to maintain. I got to 5.0 at age 39 believe and stayed there for 4 playing years. Back down to 4.5, but I’d rather play pickleball now.

15% would be a wonderful goal. But I don’t think I’ve been under 150 pounds since 7th or 8th grade.

That’s great – pickleball is fun too and more social. Plus you can be out there for hours and hours. I played on the club tennis team at USC a long time ago, now just play recreationally and through leagues when my schedule allows

#8452. Investing Isn’t Gambling – Hold Index Funds for Decades and Cap Bets at 5%

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Owning a diversified stock fund for years isn’t gambling. The companies in a fund earn profits that give it a positive average return, while casinos set up their games so players lose on average. Put your long-term money in the fund, and keep bets on next week’s price to a small slice you could lose entirely.

Judged one year at a time, the stock market can look like a casino. Large U.S. stocks, measured by the S&P 500 with dividends included, lost money in 26 of the 98 years from 1928 through 2025, according to year-by-year returns compiled by NYU Stern professor Aswath Damodaran.

Over all 98 years, though, they returned about 10% a year before inflation, because the companies behind them earn profits, pay part out as dividends, and reinvest the rest to grow. Holding longer is what makes the gain dependable. With dividends reinvested and before inflation, every 20-year stretch in the data, all 79 of them, ended with a gain. The worst, 1929 through 1948, still turned $1,000 into about $1,600.

At the roulette table, time works against you. On an American wheel, the house keeps about 5.26% of the money bet on red, according to Britannica, so a $1,000 bet there loses about $53 on average. The more spins you play, the closer your results get to losing 5.26% of everything you bet.

The line between investing and gambling is where the payoff comes from. Investing pays you from the profits that companies earn over years. A broad index fund owns hundreds of those companies at once by holding every stock in an index such as the S&P 500.

A bet on next week’s price or on a single hot stock is gambling, because it pays only if the price moves your way in time. So is buying options that expire in days, contracts that become worthless unless the stock passes a set price by then.

If you want to place those bets, use only money you could lose entirely, cap it at 5% of what you invest, and keep it in a separate account. Count any crypto you buy in that slice too.

Put everything else you invest in a broad index fund, and don’t sell it in the losing years, since every one of those 79 stretches had at least two.

Compare the best online brokers to pick where to buy that fund.

Your gut tells you to sell after a drop and buy after a run-up, the reverse of buying low and selling high. While you’re calm, write a one-page plan that sets your mix of stocks and bonds, monthly buys, rebalancing date, and reasons to sell. Then automate what you can and follow the plan, not your gut.

The S&P 500 index fell about a third from its Feb. 19, 2020, peak to its March 23 low, and investors who sold that day locked in the loss. By Aug. 18, the index had rallied more than 50% to a record close.

Selling felt safe that day because instinct is built to run from danger and chase what’s working. Four biases explain how it shows up in your trades.

Loss aversion makes a loss hurt more than an equal gain feels good, so a falling balance pushes you to sell just to stop the pain. Recency bias makes you expect the last few months to continue, so a slump feels endless and a hot streak feels safe. Herd behavior has you buy what everyone else is buying, usually after it has already run up. And after one good call, overconfidence makes you trust the next hunch more than it deserves.

The fix is to make each decision once, on a calm day, and write it down. Your one-page plan should cover four things:

Then automate as much of the plan as you can. A robo-advisor can manage your mix and rebalance it for you, which leaves you fewer choices to make during a market scare.

Finally, add a cooling-off rule. Before any trade your plan doesn’t call for, wait 48 hours and reread it.

#8450. Controversy Continues on Dhaulagiri as Expeditions Called Off

After Manaslu, Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er this season with no summits. The rope-fixing team says they stopped working for safety reasons, but some climbers suspect other motivations and describe a tense atmosphere.

Paul Clarke of Australia — who had been waiting at Camp 2 for five days — shared his frustrations with ExplorersWeb. Clarke had just learned that the rope fixers had stopped working above Camp 3 and were retreating. He described a lack of motivation among the Sherpa rope fixers after VIP clients with Seven Summit Treks, the company in charge of fixing the route, had called off their summit attempt. Soon after, all 20 climbers waiting at Camp 2 were told to return to Base Camp.

“Makalu Lakpa came through the lower camp this morning after the decision had been made,” Clarke said. “It was a pretty uncomfortable atmosphere, and I think everyone understands just how badly this has affected the rest of the teams on the mountain.”

Clarke’s outfitter, 8K Expeditions, sent a Sherpa team to retrieve their gear and tents from Camp 3 at 7,100m.

A helicopter lands at Dhaulagiri Base Camp. Photo: Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

Makalu Lakpa Sherpa is leading the 14 Peaks Dhaulagiri Expedition, one of the two largest teams, together with its sister company, Seven Summit Treks. Today, he posted a message explaining that increasing winds on October 10 resulted in a higher risk of slab avalanches on October 11, when his team was due to attempt the summit. He says that is the only reason his team returned to Base Camp.

In an unusual remark, Lakpa stated that he looks after his own group and cannot be held responsible for “other teams’ summit ambitions, climbing strategies, or rope-fixing arrangements.” He also noted that the rope-fixing work was assigned to Seven Summit Treks, not his team.

Finally, he spoke out against climbers who had expressed their disagreement yesterday:

To those criticizing our decision from a distance, I ask you to understand the actual mountain conditions before passing judgment. Assessing risks firsthand and making decisions that determine whether a team returns home safely is very different from commenting on social media.

Guides working for Lakpa’s company and for Seven Summit Treks have posted messages on social media supporting his decision. Benny Lieber, an American guide working for 14 Peaks, posted his assessment of avalanche risks on the mountain:

A post on Dhaulagiri conditions by Benny Lieber on Instagram. Photo: Benny Lieber/Instagram

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, leader of Seven Summit Treks, argued that the weather window was too short, given that a summit push would take “several days.” The plan was to move up to Camp 3 on October 11, reach the summit on the morning of October 12 (with October 13 as a buffer day), and return to Base Camp the following day.

Chhang Dawa, a director at Seven Summit Treks, posted about Dhaulagiri’s weather forecasts. Photo: Chhang Dawa/Instagram

Still, these explanations have not satisfied some climbers. Their biggest frustration came from watching the mountain in perfect, windless weather (though a wind plume eventually grew on the summit, according to Benny Lieber).

“From my perspective, one of the biggest frustrations is how badly the weather window appears to have been misread by Makalu Sherpa,” Paul Clarke said. “The strong winds and poor climbing conditions yesterday were not a surprise, since we had all been watching the forecasts for days, and winds in the 40–50kph range had been clearly visible well in advance.

“Despite that, Makalu Sherpa sent the rope-fixing team and his VIP clients higher on the mountain yesterday in conditions that were obviously going to be difficult. That has left climbers from multiple other operators stranded by a decision they had no control over. The consequence is that the rope-fixing team has now come back down, the VIP clients are no longer continuing [a helicopter was waiting for them as they arrived in Base Camp], and we have just been told that all our expeditions are over.”

Vincere Zeng of Singapore also shared her pòint of view with ExplorersWeb. Zeng has summited seven 8,000’ers, and was the first Singaporean woman to summit K2 and Annapurna. “I attempted it [Dhaulagiri] last autumn as well, so I was fully aware of the risks involved, which is why I had been monitoring the weather closely every day,” she said.

Zeng explained that her group was aware of high winds on October 9 and 10, and therefore waited at Camp 2. They planned to attempt the summit today, on October 12, in the morning. “We also considered Oct 12-13 as a possible buffer, as the next strong wind cycle was forecast to arrive around the afternoon of Oct 14,” Zeng explained.

“What I did not understand was why the 14 Peaks team chose to move toward Camp 3 (~7,000m) on Oct 10, which was the windiest day in the forecast, and then cancelled the rope fixing based on the conditions they encountered that day,” Zeng said. “From our side, we hoped we would at least have the opportunity to assess conditions during the originally planned Oct 11-12 window.”

Both Clarke and Zeng said that the 8K Sherpas who went to Camp 3 yesterday to retrieve equipment reported good conditions to that point.

“Of course, that does not mean conditions higher up, particularly around the traverse and summit slopes, were necessarily safe,” Zeng noted. “But it was one reason I hoped conditions could be reassessed once the forecasted wind had passed, especially as we still had time to do so. Instead, we were informed that the expedition was cancelled before we had that opportunity.”

Vincere Zeng (with green down suit) waits at Camp 2 in good weather last weekend. Photo: Vincere Zeng

Zeng explained she was “absolutely prepared to turn around if an assessment showed that conditions were unsafe.”

Clarke confirmed that all commercial expeditions on Dhaulagiri have called off their attempts. With the big teams pulling out, there is no manpower to launch another commercial-style attempt.

“At this point, nearly all of the teams have already packed up their Base Camp operations, and almost all of the climbers have flown out by helicopter, either yesterday afternoon or this morning,” Clarke said.

One team, however, has no intention of leaving. Andrzej Bargiel’s expedition, which includes a significant support team and film crew, is still hoping to summit and ski down the mountain, as he explained to fellow climber Xenia Santha of Hungary today.

“We wish Andrzej [Bargiel] the best of luck,” Clarke said. “If he can continue and summit, it will obviously provide another very clear picture of what the conditions on the mountain were actually like during this window.”

Risk assessment is always a tricky issue on commercial expeditions. Climbers pay large sums of money and expect every possible summit chance. It is often hard to explain when conditions are too risky, considering that factors include avalanche risks and wind, but also group sizes, the skills and endurance of guided climbers, complex logistics, and the disastrous consequences of a wrong decision.

However, in this instance, it is the lack of choices rather than the conditions that has frustrated climbers. Ironically, commercial expeditions on big mountains are more interdependent that ever, but communication between them, and sometimes with their clients, can be poor.

“As a client, I have no exact knowledge of the rope-fixing arrangement or collaboration agreed between the different outfitters,” Zeng said. “As we were a relatively small team with less manpower [8K Expeditions], we were to some extent dependent on the main rope-fixing team and whatever cooperation had been agreed between the operators. So, once the main fixing effort stopped, in practical terms it also affected our ability to continue.”

“Seven Summit Treks and Makalu Lakpa are now, from our perspective, trying to justify the decisions that were made by saying the weather was the reason they stopped,” Clarke concluded after reading the posts by Makalu Lakpa and Chhang Dawa today. “Based on the forecasts we had been watching for days, what we saw ourselves, and now the reports from climbers and Sherpas who were actually higher on the mountain, I simply don’t agree with that explanation.”

Large expedition operators sometimes react only when climbers openly share their experiences and thoughts, and their reaction is often to try to stop the dissemination of news from the mountains.

Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha, said media coverage had caused tension. Santha received a text message asking why she and Clarke had been speaking to the press. “I found that quite surprising; we have only spoken publicly about what we experienced firsthand and about decisions that directly affected our expedition,” Clarke said.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8449. Beware, A Disability Can Force You Into Early Retirement

Earlier this year, I was sick for two weeks. Unfortunately, I’ve had asthma since I was a kid. So when a respiratory illness hits, I tend to cough and suffer longer than the average person.

During COVID, my asthma flared up more often, likely due to the stress of having a baby during a pandemic.

It’s the type of breathing where you’re annoyingly conscious of every breath. You can never quite fill your lungs to 100%. In my case, it felt more like 75%.

On Wednesday, August 12, still sick, I decided to keep a previously scheduled consulting call with an FS reader. I had booked it assuming I’d be better by then. I wasn’t.

By the end of our 1 hour, 15 minute session, where I spent about 80% of the time talking, I was wiped out. My energy had dropped to maybe 30%. When you’re talking nonstop, you’re not breathing deeply or regularly. I felt like I was slowly suffocating while discussing their asset allocation.

The call reminded me of the many days I felt physically drained talking to clients during my 13 years in finance. As my responsibilities and stress grew, I eventually hit a breaking point. I’d rather earn nothing and be free and healthy than keep grinding myself down.

Just the other day, I couldn’t bend down to pick something up without a sharp pain shooting through my spine. I almost collapsed.

The last time I felt pain this bad was in 2023. I had spent an hour sitting on the ground signing copies of Buy This Not That for readers who donated to victims of the Maui fires. My dad is from Hawaii, and seeing thousands of lives upended overnight weighed on me. The Financial Samurai community ended up donating about $48,000. But when the signing was over, I couldn’t stand up and I called my wife for help.

My theory is that these episodes are triggered by a combination of prolonged stress and me forgetting I’m not 25 anymore.

This time, I clearly forgot. On Sunday, I played two hours of 4.5-level pickleball, then taught my kids for another hour. On Monday, I played 1.5 hours of intense tennis with plenty of serving. Then on Tuesday, several dads in our dad bod challenge shared their gym Personal Records, so naturally I went for personal records too. Instead of my usual three sets of 10-12 reps, I did five sets with progressive loading.

Wednesday morning, my back was already grumbling. So of course I went on a hilly 30-minute walk at 7:05am before breakfast and the school drop off. Walking downhill to school, the pain returned. By the time I got home, I could no longer walk normally.

If I still had a day job, there’s no way I could have gone into the office. And if my asthma flared up at the same time, I couldn’t speak to clients for more than an hour or two a day.

Not being able to provide for my family would be a terrible thing.

These two episodes forced me to confront a few uncomfortable truths:

Some people picture disability as a dramatic car accident or a fall off a ladder. Reality is far more boring. Accidental injuries make up only about 9% to 12% of long-term disability claims, while musculoskeletal problems like back and joint pain are the leading cause, at 26% to 33% of claims.

According to the Social Security Administration (SSA), roughly one in four 20-year-olds will be out of work for at least a year because of a disabling condition before reaching normal retirement age. That’s one quarter of all 20-year-olds, not just those in high-risk occupations.

In other words, the thing that takes you out of the workforce probably won’t be a skydiving mishap. It’ll be your back after one too many weightlifting attempts.

Before getting into what to do, it’s worth understanding the two main types of disability coverage. They work very differently.

Short-term disability (STD) covers you for a temporary inability to work, like recovering from surgery, a bad back, or a serious illness. Benefits typically replace around 50% to 70% of your income and last anywhere from a few weeks to about six months. The waiting period, called the elimination period, is usually short, often one to two weeks.

Many employers provide short-term disability as a benefit. A handful of states also run their own programs, including California (SDI), New York, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Hawaii (TDI). If you’re self-employed, you probably have nothing unless you bought it yourself.

Long-term disability (LTD) kicks in when a disability lasts longer, usually after a 90-day elimination period. It typically replaces about 60% of your income and can pay for a set number of years or until age 65. This is the coverage that actually protects your family’s financial future. Short-term disability is a speed bump. Long-term disability is a car crash.

And no, don’t count on Social Security Disability Insurance to save you. SSDI is hard to qualify for, has a five-month waiting period, and the monthly benefit is modest. It’s a floor, not a plan.

If you have a job with benefits, log into your HR portal today and look at your LTD coverage. Many group policies cap monthly benefits, which means high earners may only be replacing a fraction of their income.

If there’s a gap, buy a supplemental individual policy, ideally with an own-occupation rider. It’s portable, so it stays with you if you leave your job. If you’re self-employed like me, individual LTD is the only coverage you’ll have. Get quotes while you’re young and healthy, because pre-existing conditions get excluded or priced up later.

Even with great coverage, there’s a gap. Short-term disability might make you wait a week or two, and long-term disability usually makes you wait 90 days. Meanwhile, your mortgage, tuition, and Costco runs don’t pause.

Keep at least six months of living expenses in cash or Treasury bills. If you have kids, a single income household, or are self-employed, aim for 12 months. If you’re wondering where the line is between prudent and paranoid, here’s my take on how much savings is too much. The emergency fund is your bridge from healthy to covered.

A single income stream is a single point of failure. If that engine stalls, the whole plane goes down. Your goal is to build a jet with at least four engines, so you can lose one and still land safely.

The best time to start a side hustle is while you still have a steady paycheck and good health. You get to experiment without pressure, and if it fails, you still eat.

I started Financial Samurai in July 2009 while working full-time in finance. I’d wake up early and write before work, then publish again on weekends. For three years, it made very little money. But by the time I left Corporate America in 2012, the site had become a real second engine alongside about $80,000 a year in passive investment income.

Without that second engine, I never would have had the courage to negotiate my way out.

Here’s the key for disability planning: prioritize side hustles that don’t require your body to show up. Driving for Uber or coaching tennis stops the moment your back gives out. Writing, a blog, a YouTube channel, an online course, or a self-published ebook can keep paying while you’re flat on your back.

If you need ideas, my wife put together a list of the 20 best side hustle ideas to make extra money. If you want to go the online route, here’s how to start a blog and build your own platform. I’m biased, but owning your own corner of the internet is the gift that keeps on giving.

One engine is a job. Two engines is a cushion. Four or more engines is freedom.

Your peak earning years are also, conveniently, your peak health years. Don’t assume your income will keep climbing forever. Assume it could drop to zero tomorrow, then save as if that’s true.

Related: Achieving FI With A Visual Impairment

I saved over 50% of my after-tax income starting with my first job out of college because I knew I couldn’t last a lifetime working 70+ hours a week. I didn’t know my lungs and back would eventually join the protest, but the logic held up.

Front-load your savings. Max out your 401(k) and IRA, and invest the excess in a taxable brokerage account. Pay down high fixed costs where you can.

The lower your required monthly expenses, the less income replacement you need if disaster strikes. A paid-off house is one of the best disability insurance policy nobody talks about.

Your ability to earn over the next 20 to 30 years is likely worth millions. Yet we manage our portfolios more carefully than our bodies.

Get annual checkups. But lock down a life insurance policy before you see a doctor for something more. Manage your stress before it manages you. Warm up, cool down, and stop trying to beat the other dads’ PRs after a weekend of nonstop racquet sports. Ask me how I know.

While you’re at it, get your paperwork in order. A will, a durable power of attorney, and a healthcare directive are the basics. But if anyone depends on your income, term life insurance is the most important piece. A disability takes away your ability to earn for a while. Death takes it away for good.

The irony is that the health problems that make you worry about disability also make life insurance more expensive, or harder to get. Lock in coverage while you’re still healthy enough to qualify. I’d compare term life quotes on Policygenius, which lets you see prices from multiple top insurers in one place.

The scary thing about disability is that it rarely announces itself. One day you’re serving aces and going for gym PRs. The next, you can’t walk your kids to school.

Being unable to breathe normally or walk for a few days made me realize how fragile everything is. If you’re the provider for your family, that fragility is your responsibility to plan for.

So check your disability coverage this week. Build your cash buffer. Start a side hustle that doesn’t depend on your body showing up. And for goodness sake, stretch.

Have you ever been unable to work for an extended period due to an illness or injury? Do you know whether your employer’s long-term disability policy is own-occupation or any-occupation, and when it switches? How many engines of income do you have today, and which would keep running if you couldn’t get out of bed? Have you bought supplemental disability insurance, or do you think it’s a waste of money? And what side hustle would you start if your main income disappeared tomorrow?

The own-occupation versus any-occupation distinction was the part that stood out most to me, since a policy that only pays when you cannot do any job is far weaker than it first sounds. Your point about the waiting period also deserves more attention, because even a good policy leaves a gap that only a cash buffer can cover. This was a useful reminder to check the fine print on my own coverage this week rather than assuming it is enough.

I had a concussion which another cyclist collided into me over a decade ago. I was 54 yrs. I lost my memory for 4 hrs. and have no memory of people helping to get off bike path, transported by ambulance to hospital, etc. It was like the movies…I woke up in pain and was on a spinal bord in ICU ward, with my partner and neurology dr. bending over, testing my memory after I awoke. I had to learn to walk slowly in lst few wks., I was dizzy just standing in the shower or in front of my kitchen sink, turning. I had to rest for many hours in bed for well over a month. If I walked too fast, I got dizzy from seeing blur of colours of scenery around me, etc. Thankfully as part of employer’s benefit, I had short-term disability insurance which I had to tap into long-term disability insurance. I returned to work lst part-time after 5 months on disability /medical leave. I returned to cycling slowly at 6 months. My partner did all the housework, cooking and food shopping during my recovery. It took me another few additional months to become comfortable even having other cyclists cycle around me.

It scared the beejesus out of me, because I solo paying off my home mortgage. My partner was still paying off his. This is what happens when you are solely responsible for your own mortgage or any huge loan/debt. Your financial vulnerability becomes even more acutely real. Thankfully at that time, I had a reverse mortgage.

I so strongly recommend any worker get disability insurance..and if you don’t have children, you don’t have to worry about life insurance. There’s far greater likelihood during your working years, you will not prematurely die young but more likely to have major injury/ surgery (broken leg, hip replacement, etc.) that will sideline you from your job for a few months or a yr. All of us, even the most healthy (like myself) will experience a major injury/illness where we can’t do our money-earning job.

I’m glad you are now OK and had insurance when that accident happened!

Sam, this article really hit home for me. At age 55, I began experiencing symptoms of an extremely rare disease. After years of uncertainty, dozens of doctors, and losing nearly 40 pounds, I suffered a stroke at 57 that abruptly ended my career in construction management and real estate development. Fortunately, the stroke spared my speech, cognition, and memory, but permanently impaired my left-side motor control and sensation. Thirteen years later, chronic pain, spasticity, and mobility limitations remain daily challenges. One lesson I’d emphasize is the importance of good health insurance. Medical bills totaled approximately $675,000 over four years, including $485,000 leading up to and including the stroke. Even with insurance, some rehabilitation required appeals or out-of-pocket payments. My stroke also forced me to sell my interest in our development business to my longtime partner. Although we had planned for a buyout in the event of death, disability was a different matter, and we ultimately negotiated an amicable agreement. I was fortunate to have accumulated substantial savings and investments before becoming disabled. Equally important, I was blessed with supportive family and friends, including a sister who’s a professional financial advisor, a physician brother-in-law, a daughter who’s an ER nurse, and a son who’s a mental health therapist. Unable to return to work, I focused more on managing our investments. With my sister’s guidance, we maintained a buy-and-hold approach through major market downturns. I’m a testament to time in the market, not timing the market, and the power of compounding. Our net worth has more than tripled since before the stroke. Meanwhile, rehabilitation remains a lifelong project. Now 71, I recently returned to my longtime neurological physical therapist after a three-year break. I’m still looking for ways to improve my independence, mobility, and quality of life. Forced retirement at 57 certainly didn’t mean the end of a productive and purposeful life. Financial independence can’t restore your health, but it provides options when life changes unexpectedly. My advice: Save and invest early, maintain good insurance, appreciate your support network, and don’t postpone enjoying life while you’re healthy.

Thank you for sharing your experience. It really hits Home, the importance of good health, good health insurance, and spending more intentionally with our one and only lives.

I wish you good health and prosperity. Don’t be a stranger!

My wife has been on disability for 10 years. She was a teacher before, so I was the breadwinner. Luckily, I had suspected some illnesses so I had signed up for her for an employer disability policy. I’ve also had her records well organized so we got approved on social security disability under first pass. I also took out a long-term care insurance policy years before, but I haven’t used it yet.

The thing with health insurance is that you can just buy it on the exchange. It’s an extra cost of maybe three to $4000 a month. Once you bake that into your expenses, it’s just life as usual.

At 51, if you have the money, I would spend it on freedom. You have maybe 20 years until you can’t really spend your money anymore.

I just took a medical retirement (disability) from my employer (Fire Service) and I completely agree with all your points. You MUST know your benefits and if your employer doesn’t have sufficient benefits for you, you MUST seek them out on your own on the private market. While my profession is dangerous and premiums can be high, most other professions premiums are very reasonable for the protection you get. My terms are; 60% of my last years salary (tax free) own occ for 3 years, then any occ till age 65. I will add that my plan has a max benefit which I exceeded because my salary was over the max. Due to being tax free, it is a solid benefit but not something at all that I wanted to do. There’s alot of admin and jumping through hoops and restrictions on working for me going forward. One thing this has probably been the biggest challenge is the mental side of it. Injury/disease is very, very difficult mentally, especially for active people, and something that should not be underestimated. I miss my job quite alot, although I don’t miss the politics one bit. I absolutely am a person that needs to engage with other people and that can be a challenge sometimes when everyone else is at work. A final thought; The ONLY way my family is able to adjust to this new situation is because we have invested aggressively outside my modest pension, much to the lessons written by this newsletter over the years. Sam, I truly have learned alot from you and am grateful.

“ One thing this has probably been the biggest challenge is the mental side of it. Injury/disease is very, very difficult mentally, especially for active people, and something that should not be underestimated.”

Agree with lots of these points. I think it’s really important to protect yourself & your family from the downside of bad events like long term illness. I’m based in the UK, so the products are different, but I think it’s key to have long term income protection, critical illness protection and life insurance protection for the household in general. You don’t need it until you do…

In the UK we also have income protection that can cover redundancy for 12 months. I have that too. That’s happened to me twice over my career and certainly glad I had it. Had to plan for a wedding while unemployed and not having the redundancy pay from my income protection+ savings would have made life a lot harder than it was already.

Could be. Did you find joy or relief in finding out you have a disc bulge and couldn’t do anything about it?

I really like the book, Healing Back Pain by Dr. Sarno. It got rid of my back pain of 2-3 years back in 2001-2003, and I had been largely back pain free until 2023 and then recently.

It gave me relief in knowing my issue wasnt worse and then after addl research realizing how many people have bulges and herniations without pain. I’m still dealing with my pain but looking forward to 1% improvement every week. Thanks for the book recommendation- I’ll start reading it today.

Enjoy! One of its recommendations is actually to not get an MRI. I think you’ll enjoy the book.

I went through all of my 20s and most of my 30s before I understood what disability insurance is and the difference between short-term and long-term. I had those benefits from my employer, but never took the time to really understand what they were or appreciate having that type of coverage.

And yeah, it’s so true that needing it can be something completely unexpected and isn’t always catastrophic. I’ve had friends who needed to use short term for everything from foot surgery to abdominal surgery to mat leave. And I remember reading that article featuring a guest author about how he needed long-term disability for vision loss. That was a very moving and eye-opening story.

Nobody wants to have to need insurance, but it sure can be a lifesaver.

It’s true that physical disability is not always dramatic. I’ve lost a career or income twice due to physical disability, but I am actually pretty healthy and active. One was due to allergies and asthma developing when I was in the military. The second was due to developing severe arthritis in my elbow when I was working the twilight shift at UPS and taking care of my kids during the day. A couple of things helped. During the five years I worked the twilight shift, my wife was working too, and I effectively saved and invested all of my salary. I had been pivoting into the professional side of the military and had used my GI Bill for training, but the civilian side wasn’t a good fit, so I used tuition reimbursement to start working on an accounting degree in my spare time. I didn’t have additional capacity for a side hustle, but I ran the numbers and determined that if I lost my warehouse job and benefits, my best course of action was not to take another part time blue collar job at entry level, but to finish my degree as quickly as possible. When I was injured, I had a plan and leaned into it right away. That’s where I am right now, and I’m graduating in March.

Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

The booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

Before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Log into your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. If you don't have 17,500 miles already, check your transferable points balances:

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

If you're struggling to find seats close to your travel dates, shift your strategy to the booking window's leading edge. Virgin opens award availability 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date, log in at that exact time, and book the moment inventory releases. Peak-season seats to popular destinations like Rome and Athens move quickly.

After booking, screenshot your confirmation, note your booking reference, and verify the routing, cabin class, and surcharge amounts. Add the flight to your calendar with the Virgin Atlantic booking reference. Sign up for flight notifications.

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

Let's walk through a real scenario that illustrates exactly what this redemption looks like in practice.

The Setup: You've just arrived at London Heathrow on a transatlantic award — perhaps an ANA First Class redemption through the very same Flying Club program. You have a few days in London, and now you need to get to Athens, Greece, where your Mediterranean adventure begins. You check flights: a business class seat on Virgin Atlantic's LHR → ATH route on your target date is priced at $2,200 cash.

The Redemption: You log into virginatlantic.com and find a business class award seat on that same flight: 17,500 Virgin miles + approximately $120 in taxes and fuel surcharges. You have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your ThankYou account from your Citi Premier card. You initiate the transfer — 1:1, instant — and within minutes, your Flying Club account reflects 17,500 miles (with 2,500 to spare for future use). You complete the booking.

The Experience: On the day of travel, you access the Virgin Clubhouse at Heathrow — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world. The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Do this: Search 331 days out for peak season Virgin's booking window opens exactly 331 days before departure. For summer travel to Athens, Rome, or other peak European destinations, business class award inventory gets claimed early. Set a phone reminder 331 days before your ideal travel date. Log in that morning. The seats that seem impossible to find in the 60-day window are often available the moment the calendar rolls over.

Do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. If you send 17,500 Chase points over and then discover the seat isn't actually available (or you misread the cabin class), those miles are stuck in Flying Club. Always — always — confirm the specific flight and cabin availability first, THEN transfer.

Avoid this: Confusing this with partner award bookings Virgin's zero-surcharge policy applies to partner airlines like ANA and Delta. On Virgin Atlantic-operated flights (which this redemption is), expect fuel surcharges of $50–$150. Budget for these. They don't destroy the CPP math, but they're a genuine cash cost you need to plan around.

Do this: Hold Virgin miles for multiple redemptions Because miles don't expire with account activity every 36 months, there's no reason to hoard and rush. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

This redemption is built for a specific type of ChooseFI traveler: the intermediate-to-advanced points strategist who thinks in itineraries, not individual flights.

The ideal candidate is someone who's already planning a trip that routes through London Heathrow — perhaps on a transatlantic award — and needs an elegant, high-value way to reach their final European destination. Solo travelers and couples benefit most here. At 17,500 miles per person, a couple needs 35,000 Virgin miles, which is completely achievable with a single transfer from a combined Chase or Amex balance.

Families should approach with caution. This redemption scores a 2/5 for family-friendliness for good reason. Multiplying 17,500 miles per person across four or more travelers creates a significant points requirement, and availability for multiple seats on the same flight is far from guaranteed. The fuel surcharges also multiply with passenger count. Families are better served by other redemption strategies.

This is NOT for beginners. The overall score of 2.7/5 and beginner-friendliness rating of 1/5 signal real complexity. If you're just starting your travel rewards journey, build your foundation with simpler redemptions first. But if you've got a year of points accumulation behind you and you're ready to think architecturally about trip planning, this sweet spot can be a revelatory experience.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally shows availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

Log into VirginAtlantic.com and search for reward flights in Upper Class (business) on your desired European route. Look for VS-coded flights only. Ignore partner-operated results, which will price differently.

Midweek flights (Tuesday through Thursday) and shoulder season dates offer the best availability. Peak summer weekends and holiday periods are harder to find. Build flexibility into your schedule if possible.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Flying Club are instant, making Chase the preferred transfer partner for time-sensitive bookings. Amex Membership Rewards also transfers 1:1 but may take 1-2 days.

Complete the booking on VirginAtlantic.com. Your business class ticket includes access to the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse at Heathrow, one of the best airport lounges in Europe. Arrive early and enjoy it as part of the experience.

Virgin Atlantic operates short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations including Amsterdam, Paris CDG, Edinburgh, Geneva, Athens, Tel Aviv, and several others. Routes change seasonally, so check VirginAtlantic.com for current schedules. The 17,500-point sweet spot applies to all Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class flights.

Yes, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices awards as one-way, so you can book a single short-haul business class segment for 17,500 points. This makes it ideal for positioning flights where you only need one direction covered by points.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. You get dedicated check-in, priority boarding, the Heathrow Clubhouse lounge (which is excellent), a meal service, and a more relaxed travel experience. At 17,500 points, the per-point value (3-5 cents) makes it a strong redemption even for a short flight.

Virgin Atlantic does add taxes and fees to award tickets, including some carrier-imposed surcharges. On short-haul European routes, total out-of-pocket costs typically run $50-$150 depending on the route and departure airport taxes. This is higher than some programs but still reasonable given the business class product.

The Virgin Atlantic short-haul European business class sweet spot is the perfect complement to a transatlantic award trip. At just 17,500 points, it costs less than most domestic economy awards while delivering business class service, Heathrow Clubhouse lounge access, and a stress-free connection to destinations across Europe. It is not the flashiest redemption in travel rewards, but it is one of the most practical: a building block that makes multi-city European itineraries accessible and affordable for the FI community.
