Pay at Costco with a Visa, the only credit card its U.S. warehouses take. Get the Costco Anywhere Visa if you buy gas there, since it pays 5% on up to $7,000 a year. In the warehouse its 2% only matches a no-fee 2% card, and Robinhood’s Gold card beats it at 3% for a $50 yearly membership.

So the first question is whether you buy enough Costco gas to carry its card, and the second is which Visa should pay for your cart. Costco’s gas stations accept Visa and no other credit card as well, according to Costco’s membership terms, while Costco.com also takes Mastercard.

The store’s own cards come first, then flat-rate cards that pay the same rate on every purchase, then cards that pay more as your balance at their bank grows.

Both pay cash back once a year, after the February statement closes, as a certificate you redeem at a U.S. Costco warehouse for merchandise or cash.

At 5%, a household that buys $3,000 of gas a year at Costco’s pumps earns $150 with this card, against $60 on a 2% card.

With Robinhood’s $50-a-year Gold membership, it pays 3% in the warehouse and at the pump, and after that fee it beats a no-fee 2% card once you charge it more than $5,000 a year.

Members who want one card with no annual fee and nothing else to join get 2% from it in the warehouse, at the pump, and everywhere else.

For more information, read our full Wells Fargo Active Cash® Card Review.

Fidelity investors earn 2% in the warehouse, as Costco’s own card does, but the cash back goes into a Fidelity brokerage, retirement, or college savings account instead of onto a Costco certificate.

For more information, read our full Fidelity® Rewards Visa Signature® Credit Card Review.

U.S. Bank customers with $10,000 already in Smartly Checking, and a Smartly Savings account, earn 2.5% in the warehouse, and 4% at $100,000, on up to $10,000 of purchases a billing cycle.

For more information, read our full U.S. Bank Smartly™ Visa Signature® Card Review.

Bank of America checking customers in its BofA Rewards program earn 2.2% at wholesale clubs like Costco, or 3% once their deposit and investment balances there average $100,000, up to a quarterly cap.

For more information, read our full Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards Credit Card Review.

At Costco, gas is where its own card leads, and the cart is where a flat rate or a bank balance decides what you earn. Put Costco gas on the Costco Anywhere Visa and pair it with a no-fee 2% Visa for the cart, or with the Robinhood Gold Card if you’d put over $5,000 a year on it.

#8446. A Human-Powered Journey Around Norway

Bad weather has forced Norwegian Jonas Holm, 27, to alter his 5,500km human-powered attempt to circle Norway.

Holm took a year off from his construction job and set out from southern Norway in late April, beginning in Svinesund on the Swedish border. He planned to paddle nearly 3,000km north, skirting Norway’s coastline as far as Grense Jakobselv, near the Russian border. From there, he would travel south through Norway, Finland, and Sweden with his dog, Rago.

Jonas Holm during the kayak section of his journey. Photo: Jonas Holm/Padling

However, difficult conditions forced him to stop paddling south of Bodø in northern Norway, a little over halfway to Grense Jakobselv. On his website, Holm says he wants to avoid feeling pressure to reach particular places by particular dates, instead focusing on experiencing the landscape. With constant wind and rain, he decided the remaining fiords could wait until next spring.

Holm’s tracked route so far. Photo: Jonas Holm

Holm won’t sit on the couch until he can complete the coastline. Rather than wait months for better weather, he has stored his kayak and will begin the second segment of his journey: the 2,500km trek south from Grense Jakobselv. After a quick break at home to dry his clothes and gear, Holm recently drove north to Grense Jakobselv and set out with a backpack and a companion. Rago, his Alaskan malamute, is even carrying some equipment. As winter arrives and snow accumulates, Holm plans to eventually transition from walking with a backpack to skis and a pulk.

His exact route is unclear, but he will roughly trace Norway’s eastern border, though he mentions crossing parts of Finland and Sweden on his way back to his starting point in southern Norway.

You can follow Holm’s progress through the live tracker on his expedition website.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8445. The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Social Security

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who currently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re new to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:

Whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result!  Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

The net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a big boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all issues. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that new users will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions

If you log in to check on your Social Security account when you’re still young, you’ll see some confusing stuff – basically it tells you how much your payout will be if you continue working and contributing for a ridiculously long 35 year period!Your benefit is calculated by taking an average of your 35 highest years of earnings, which sounds bleak for people like me who only worked a ten-year career, because in theory that average might contain mostly zeroes. But never fear because:

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35.  Look at the difference in their benefits:

So the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI

Even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. If you want to learn more, I’ve found the AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini or OpenAI’s Chat GPT) to be shockingly useful at answering questions and running analyses. If you haven’t started using these in your financial research, I highly recommend them. Just search for any of those names (or install the phone app), start typing your questions, and you’ll be learning at a rapid pace within moments.

This Net Present Value framework completely changes the math for me. As an active investor, I’ve been weighing whether to claim early and invest the checks or wait.

I turn 64 this November, and by delaying just one year, I effectively ‘buy’ a guaranteed, inflation-indexed ~7% bump in my benefits for life. In today’s market, where valuations feel ‘rich’ and finding a low-risk 7% return is tough, I’ve decided to apply some ‘valuation discipline.’

I’m following Warren Buffett’s lead here—holding some cash and waiting for a ‘fat pitch’ or a market correction, all while letting my Social Security asset grow safely on the sidelines at a rate the market can’t currently guarantee. Thanks for providing the framework to look at it this way

Probably better to just pick a long term asset allocation you are comfortable with holding forever.

Any “gains” you are getting by delaying social security are now lost due to your failed market timing. Hoarding cash only works if you are willing to deploy it.

Yes, Bill, that’s also how I think about it. It is not an asset I can leave to others. I’d rather use my social security and use less of my other assets so that they can continue to grow and can potentially be available to others after I die. Plus, social security only comes in one form: monthly payments. But my own savings I can access in lump sums if I want. Maybe I need to do a home repair or want to have a luxurious trip. Great article. When I was younger, I never included Social Security in my retirement planning. Something that really helped me with the mental math of Social Security is the concept of bend points.

Bend points are lifetime earnings milestones that govern how much Social Security pays out to you. For all income up to the first bend point, you get about 90 cents back from Social Security for every dollar you pay in. After that, it drops off steeply. For income between the first and second bend points, you get more like 32 cents on the dollar, and after the second bend point, you get about 15 cents.

Right now in 2026, you hit the first bend point at something like $540,000 of total lifetime earnings, and the second bend point is around $3.25 million.

The great news for early retirees is that, because Social Security’s payout formula tails off so quickly for higher earners (as you mentioned in the article), it really doesn’t matter very much that we won’t have 35 full years of contributions. Just by working a few years, we get most of the benefits. After that, it’s a game of diminishing returns where you have to work for years and years just to increase your benefit by a small amount. No thanks – I’d rather be retired!

Great question.. in the equations I showed in this article, they don’t show that more complex calculation: they are only showing how to calculate the present value of a stream of payments as it would apply *right now*.

To get the full value you need to calculate “the net present value of a 30 year stream of inflation-adjusted $5000 per month payments that starts 30 years from now”

Social security Whoa Nellie! Yes, of course you can start taking SS at age 62. As mentioned above, if you have taxable income above about $22,000, then $1 of SS is withheld per $2 of earnings above the $22,000. Not to worry, when you reach your full retirement age, you get the withheld money back. But those withheld dollars can’t be invested from age 62-67. Next, you can’t just “toss your SS check into an index fund and make 6% after inflation.” First, those capital gains might be taxed at 0, 15, or even 20%. More importantly, those are not guaranteed. Social security goes up 8% per year of delayed filing, PLUS inflation. And those increases, unlike the aforementioned index funds, are not subject to taxation along the way. So filing early and index funding vs delayed filing is comparing a speculative taxable strategy with a guaranteed tax deferred strategy.

It’s not taxable income that counts towards the $22,000, it is earned income. The two can be quite different (think dividends, interest, capital gains vs. salary).

Good points Chris, although a couple of corrections:

– as of 2026, the Social Security earnings limit has been raised to $24,480 which is a nice bump from the $22k you cited – and there’s a HUGE loophole in that number: it does not include your dividend and capital gains income, which is likely the majority of a Mustachian’s income statement by the time they reach that age!

You can certainly include NPV of SS in your Net Worth Statement. It is an Asset (it has monetary value). An asset doesn’t need to be immediately convertible to cash in order to count as an asset – there are simple examples such as a house (that takes time and has costs associated in turning the asset into ‘money’) and more complicated ones like REITs and annuities. They are all Assets as they have monetary value.

What is probably more logical to do is including SS as a Retirement Asset – or those assets you plan to live off of in retirement. This is often a different list of assets than what is in your Net Worth Statement – and is used for a different purpose (creating a stream of cash to live off of in retirement).

I’ve always questioned the “better to wait to withdraw for maximum benefits” position. That may be true for non-mustachians who need every dollar of SS to live on and are willing to work longer to maximize their annual income. But SS’s early and delayed adjustments are actuarially derived to ensure the total cost to the system is the same. Theoretically, you would receive the same amount over your lifetime. Claiming earlier is a hedge against dying young. Unless you have a crystal ball and are assured of living longer than average, it’s better to claim early and invest. I looked into this a few years ago, and came across the paper: https://crr.bc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/IB_19-18.pdf

It’s a great summary of the history of delayed and early options (early claiming was originally designed to allow the younger spouse to not be penalized for retiring with the older spouse). It also analyzes whether the assumptions for the original actuarial adjustments apply today. Summary: adjustments for taking early (65) are probably right. It’s a wash to take anytime after 65. However, higher earners live longer and delay more. If delayed adjustments were based on those who actually use it, the increase should be less. Based on increased life expectancies, wealthier individuals should wait.

I want to call out a couple considerations around the longevity of Social Security and Medicare for those in the USA.

First, there is a provision within the Social Security legislation that stipulates should Social Security funding be deficient to pay out all intended benefits, it will still pay out based on its annual tax intake. While the Social Security funding is quickly dwindling, the expectation is that the annual tax intake will continue to represent ~80% of intended benefits. Thus, even if you don’t expect Congress to actively fix Social Security funding, unless you expect Congress to actively kill Social Security then you should expect some payout.

That said, it is important to note that Medicare has no such deficiency stipulation in its legislation, so if Medicare funding becomes deficient then without an active effort from Congress it will just be gone. I know that early retirees typically plan for medical coverage between retirement and becoming Medicare eligible, but I’ve seen many assume Medicare will be there, which it may not. On one hand, ACA coverage creates a cost-capped option at age 65+, but that assumes that ACA coverage is still around. I know MMM has also suggested options such as self-funding or community plans, but I’ll warn that those are generally more viable for those early retirement years and become generally less viable for many as you get into your golden years. This is where HSAs can be really helpful, and since they can double up as 401k-like funds for non-medical expenses after 65, I really do recommend taking advantage of them as best as you can. Everyone’s costs and longevity will vary, and potentially significantly so if you require long-term care, but there is a general rule of thumb of trying to have ~$200k/person at age 65 bucketed for retirement medical expenses (premiums and out-of-pocket costs), where the expectation is that bucket should continue to grow despite withdrawals in the early years and then transition to mostly drawing down as you get further up in the years.

Please consider using a discount rate that meets the criteria of the “next best option of similar risk.” That is standard practice for discount rates. In this case, TIPS would be a natural choice. Their inflation-adjusted discount rate would be ~2%.

After all – if we’re going to neglect risk, why not use Berkshire Hathaway’s historical return of 20% per year? Or Bitcoin’s of 230% per year?

Using the proper 2% instead of 6% would lead us to the opposite conclusion as this article. That is, claiming at 62 is the WORST choice if you’ll live until 90.

I realize this might torpedo the entire article. But it’ll also lead the audience to reach better retirement conclusions.

I’m excited to see this topic! Most people I ask (including financial advisors and moneywise folks) insist that it’s almost always better to defer drawing Social Security until normal retirement age (67) or even later (70). However, most people don’t understand the time value of money! I retired four years ago at age 57 and I’m very much looking forward to drawing Social Security next year at age 62. Why? Because it’s a much, much better deal. Here’ s how it works. Using the data provided to me by the Social Security Administration, my current estimated monthly benefit amounts will be $2,513 if starting at age 62, or $3,569 if starting at age 67, and $4,425 if starting at age 70. It appears obvious that it would be best to wait for the higher amount. But it is not. Here’s why. In a zero-interest rate world, I can run a simple break-even analysis and determine that it would take me until age 78½ to come out ahead by waiting until 67 to start. It would take me until age 80½ to break even if I waited until 70 to start. With a current life expectancy for me to live until age 76½, I’m still better off to start at age 62, but only slightly. But then again, we don’t live in a zero-interest rate world! In a 4% interest rate world, these figures change dramatically. It now takes me until age 85½ to break even when starting at age 67, and until age 87 when starting at age 70. In an 8% interest rate world (The S&P 500 has averaged 10.5% annually since 1957), my break-even points are both now out beyond 100 years old. It’s really a no-brainer!

My personal take on this (and many other “catastrophic global collapse” events) is A) Basically every member of society has a vested interest in not allowing it to happen, so it’s probably not very likely, and B) if you really think it is going to happen, where you invest your money probably won’t matter, and instead you should probably invest your time and money in planning how to survive it.

There’s a whole prepper culture around this, but if you’re truly worried about it, you’d want to have some remote land with a fresh water source, with shelter, and tools, and crops, and livestock, basically you’ll want to be as self-sufficient as possible. Of course, all of that stuff does you no good if you don’t know how to use it, and if society collapses and you realize you’re missing an important tool, you can’t just order it off Amazon any more. Ultimately the conclusion I reached is essentially, “If you really want to be set up to survive the collapse of society, you need to start living like society has collapsed already.” I decided I didn’t really want to live that way, so I’ve stopped worrying about it all that much.

Hey Pete, Regarding your comment on you won’t care about the taxes on your RMDs when you’re 75 because you’ll have plenty of income. I take issue with that as a 75 year old with a six figure retirement income living a comfy life in expensive Boulder County like you. I don’t want to pay taxes to a federal government that is spending in areas that are not my values. But that’s not my main point. Only a couple people have commented on SS taxability (e.g., Jiri, Dave) aside from taxes on RMDs. Not everyone realizes that up to 85% of your SS income is taxable depending on what other kinds of annual retirement income you have. The IRS uses a formula where tax-deferred pensions, royalties, 401K distributions, and any earned income can trigger the taxability of your SS payment. The way to potentially avoid this with the present laws is to pay taxes on any future funds when you’re working, i.e., Roth contributions, Roth conversions, and backdoor Roths if you’re over the Roth eligibility limits. This works best for 1099 people, but W-2 people also can benefit from it to a lesser extent. I’m a believer it’s not how much you make, but how much you keep from the government.

However, if you are a high earner in your working years, it makes sense to max the traditional retirements accounts to avoid a (currently) 24% or 32% tax rate (which was actually quite a bit higher in the past), not worry as much about Roth, and then pay the tax on Social Security. Odds are that the tax on your Social Security will fall in the 12% bracket, or maybe 22% if you are making particularly substantial withdrawals from traditional retirement accounts.

One thing that I’m surprised this didn’t mention is the “bond effect” of the SS PV. After reading this article I did a search for “social security present value” and came across this article from Michael Kitces: https://www.kitces.com/blog/valuing-social-security-benefits-as-an-asset-on-the-household-balance-sheet/

He discusses treating the lump sum value of the SS benefit as a bond allocation in the portfolio. I get why people might say “I don’t want to think about/consider SS because I’m so young”, but I think considering it might help people make better asset allocation decisions.

Take the 30 y/o couple in your example. If the PV of their projected SS benefit is $98k and they also have $200k invested (in retirement accounts and brokerage) then their asset allocation is roughly 33% bonds and 67% everything else. If they decide to start putting part of that $200k into bonds, then they may very likely be substantially over-allocated with bonds.

#8443. New Flash Floods Disrupt Trekking Routes in Nepal

A flash flood has cut off parts of the Manaslu Circuit in a fresh blow to Nepal’s tourism industry.

This time, the flood hit the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. While not as catastrophic as the glacial lake outburst flood in the Langtang Lirung area in late August, the flooding is still severe. A landslide caused the river to swell suddenly, washing away houses and bridges and damaging a hydropower plant, the BBC reported. Authorities have not recorded any fatalities, but some farmers remain unaccounted for.

The Bhudi Gandaki River flows south from mountains in the Manaslu region, and the flood severed the popular Manaslu Circuit in several sections. The Chum Valley is currently isolated after bridges were washed away. According to the Manaslu Conservation Area Project (MCAP), all trekkers in the area are fine. The Tourism Times reports that helicopters are airlifting some tourists back to Kathmandu.

“We have decided to cancel our Manaslu and Tsum treks for this autumn season based on advice from local authorities and our internal risk assessments,” Roland Hunter of The Mountain Company told ExplorersWeb. Instead, they are offering clients a trek through Upper Mustang followed by a crossing of Thorong La, the highest point on the Annapurna Circuit.

Poor weather also closed Thorong La for weeks after a snowy spell hit Nepal’s mountains. However, the trail recently reopened, and trekking groups have crossed the pass over the last five days. “There is a trail through the snow on the pass, and after sunny weather the snow has consolidated, reducing the risk of avalanche,” Hunter explained. “The road has been washed away lower down near Chame, although the trekking trail has been repaired so it is passable for trekking groups.”

Hunter said that many trekkers are now diverting to the Annapurna Circuit, and he presumes it will be busier than ever for the next few weeks.

The Tourism Times also reports damaged trails on the Tashi Lapcha Pass, a high-altitude trekking route connecting the Rolwaling and Khumbu regions. Tashi Lapcha is one of the most challenging sections of the Great Himalaya Trail (GHT) and includes rock scrambling and fixed ropes that are currently damaged. The paper shared a report from IAM Trekking Guides:

The damaged section lies along the approach to the David Lama Bivouac shelter at Upper Jabo. Trekkers and climbers must use the fixed ropes and carefully scramble across the rocky terrain to proceed. The loss of footholds in such a steep section can increase the risk of a fall, particularly for groups carrying trekking or climbing equipment.

A damaged passage at Tashi Lapcha. Photo: IAM Trekking Guides

Those intending to hike in the area should ask their local trekking operators and tourism offices for updated information. According to India’s weather services, the monsoon officially left Nepal yesterday. Nepal’s peak trekking season begins now and lasts until the end of November.

In a big family, buying a gift for every adult adds up fast. Propose a name draw before Thanksgiving instead, where each person draws one name and buys that person a gift under a price cap you all agree on. Everyone gives and gets one gift instead of a stack, and that one can be better.

In a family of 10 adults, buying a $50 gift for each of the other nine costs every person $450, and the family $4,500 in all.

With a name draw and a $75 cap, each person spends $75 instead of $450, or $375 less, and receives one $75 gift rather than nine $50 ones.

In Deloitte’s 2026 holiday retail survey, 47% of respondents said they would rather spend more on one meaningful gift than give several smaller ones. A name draw lets everyone in the family give that kind of gift.

Propose the switch before Thanksgiving, and before anyone has bought a gift, so the family can draw names at dinner that day or online that weekend. Pitch it as less time in stores and more fun at the exchange, not as a way to save money. Then choose the format that suits your family:

A free site such as Elfster or drawnames will run a Secret Santa draw for you. Both can keep spouses from drawing each other and let each person make a wish list, so the one gift is something its recipient asked for.

Settle the rules before anyone draws. Set one cap for every gift and treat it as a limit, not a target. Decide whether the kids join the draw or still get gifts from everyone. Agree, too, that no one buys extra gifts outside the draw, since each one raises the bill again.

Send the whole family one message with the cap, the format, and a draw date already set, so all anyone has to do is say yes.

#8441. Animal Attack Roundup

We usually hear about animal attacks that happen to hikers, tourists, and other visitors to an area. But it shouldn’t be surprising that most victims are the villagers who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here is a brief summary of the incidents worldwide in the last few days.

Hippo sinks family canoe, killing three — DR Congo

A family canoe on Lake Tumba. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

A mother and two of her children died when a hippopotamus reportedly rammed their wooden canoe during a nighttime crossing of Lake Tumba. Four family members were aboard; only one survived.

Mary Thandi, 35, and her 15-year-old daughter Esther suffered serious abdominal injuries when a hippopotamus attacked them near the Thiba River in the early evening of October 10.

They were returning home with two other people, who escaped. Both victims were hospitalized. Their current condition is unknown.

George Mbae Kalubira, 60, was fatally injured after encountering a wild elephant while searching for pasture for his goats around 5 am.

A snake catcher (not the one in this story) with a cobra. Photo: Shutterstock

A snake catcher died after being bitten in southern India. Initial reports in local press did not mention the snake species or how the bite occurred.

Police said the boars initially attacked the people at the front of the group, then charged the others. The three surviving victims suffered minor injuries.

Ishu Kumar, five, was reportedly bitten on a finger near a hand pump at a local childcare center. His family alleges that staff failed to arrange immediate medical treatment and sent him home. Neighbors later advised taking him for a ritual treatment, but he died.

Angry villagers then blocked a highway with the child’s body, demanding an investigation.

Charlette Gonsalves, 51, was bitten by a venomous snake in her kitchen early one morning before sunrise. Her family initially did not recognize the injury as a snakebite.

She was transferred between three hospitals as her condition deteriorated, but died the following morning.

A 44-year-old man was cutting grass near a pond in Đồng Tháp Province when a green snake bit his hand.

According to Vietnamese reporting, he became dizzy within three minutes and began vomiting blood approximately 20 minutes after the bite. He developed serious blood-clotting abnormalities and swelling extending toward his elbow.

Doctors administered antivenom and plasma. He survived.

The victim began vomiting, lost consciousness, and developed severe cardiovascular and neurological complications. He died approximately 83 hours after the bite.

#8440. A Landlord’s Moral Dilemma When Tenants Strike It Rich

With Anthropic’s S-1 now filed with the SEC, over 5,000 employees are about to become extremely wealthy. We’re talking about the median employee making $3 million to $10 million within three years, and likely at least a thousand people making well into eight figures or more.

The numbers behind it are astounding. The filing shows $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, up from about $1.2 billion a year earlier. Since Opus 5.5 launched on September 22, 2026, token usage for Claude has grown roughly 3.6X. The company has over $130 billion in cash and investments, is already generating an operating profit, and is about to raise $80+ billion more in its IPO. Pretty darn impressive.

For employees, making that much money in so little time is like winning the lottery. They picked the right ship, and plenty of talented people tried and couldn’t get on. With proper financial management, they and their children should be set for life.

For the rest of us commoners, luck is harder to come by.

We can buy real estate in the cities where AI companies are headquartered and hope the wealth trickles into home prices and rents. We can invest in private and public venture capital and hope the general partners pick the right companies. But even then, our exposure won’t come close to that of early AI employees who got equity as part of their paycheck.

As an unemployed dad with two young kids, I worry about falling into the permanent underclass as AI wealth pulls further ahead. It doesn’t help that I’m facing a liquidity crunch again, thanks to venture capital calls that came in much faster than expected.

So I’ve been combing through every income stream I have, looking for ways to earn more. And one stream stood out: rental property.

San Francisco rents are surging. My tenants are paying about $1,250 a month below what I could likely get today. That’s $15,000 a year, which would cover a meaningful chunk of my next capital call.

Rich tenants are growing everywhere in San Francisco right now. When the people renting your house are suddenly worth millions, it’s easy to think: they won’t even notice a few hundred extra dollars a month. Meanwhile, I’d notice it every single month given I'm cash strapped at 49.

So naturally, I got to wondering. If your tenants suddenly strike it rich, does that change what they owe you? At the very least, should they at least pay market rent?

Plenty of landlords would say yes. Being a landlord is a business, not a charity. If the market is hot and tenants can afford it, why not raise to market rent if possible? The answer is not as simple as I initially thought.

After a down period in 2022 and 2023, the San Francisco housing market is hot thanks to the AI boom.

San Francisco now has the strongest housing market in the country. Citywide rents are up about 27% year over year, with one-bedrooms up 25.4% and two-bedrooms up 26.8% all according to Zumper. This is the latest rent growth of the 100 largest U.S. cities.

Home prices are surging too. The median San Francisco home (includes condos) sold for about $1.69 million in September, up 14.7% year over year, the fastest growth of any major market. For single-family houses, the median is up about 24% (~$2.2 million), with 86% selling over asking.

So any San Francisco landlord who signed a lease in 2025 or earlier is likely no longer charging market rent. Not even close.

I’ve been a San Francisco landlord since 2005, when I rented out the first property I bought in 2003. Over the years, I’ve developed harmonious relationships with my tenants thanks to a lease that sets expectations clearly.

One of those expectations is a schedule of rents for the next three years in the lease so both tenants and landlord can budget. The increases are capped at 3% a year despite not being under rent control.

The schedule is intended to provide clarity and rewards tenants for following the lease. If tenants are in good standing, I follow the schedule each year. The longer the tenants stay, the greater discount they get compared to market. If not, I’m free to raise the rent within the law with proper written notice.

Every prospective tenant has appreciated this clarity. And even though a landlord usually leaves money on the table by raising rent below market, the peace that results is usually worth more than the extra dollars.

When it comes to owning physical real estate as part of your retirement portfolio, the biggest battle is having the patience to hold for as long as possible. Owning rental property is a war of attrition, and my faith in humanity has been tested a couple times as a landlord.

In July 2025, my tenants of 1.2 years gave notice. That was disappointing because I thought they’d stay for three years. In fact, 2025 was a turbulent year with three tenant turnovers. That’s life as a landlord. You either sell or find new tenants, and I’ve learned a few strategies on how to minimize vacancy.

For this property, the previous tenants were paying $9,200 a month. I decided to test the market at $9,995. In three weeks, I found great tenants, a couple with no pets who wanted the entire five-bedroom, four-bathroom house to themselves. Two home offices, a gym, and ocean views were on their wish list. Yes, all types of people spend six figures a year on rent.

Since then, the rental market has strengthened. I could most likely rent the house for $11,000 to $12,000 a month today. Let’s call it $11,500, to be conservative. But when the one-year anniversary came on October 1, 2026, the rent only went up to $10,250, a 2.5% increase. True to the lease, I followed the schedule because the tenants were in good standing.

The cost of following the schedule is about $1,250 a month, or $15,000 a year. And the longer the tenants stay, the bigger the opportunity cost for me, but the greater the benefit for them. So think twice before writing a fixed rent schedule for new tenants. Instead of three years, consider two. And instead of a fixed 2.5% increase, consider a range for more flexibility. Either way, setting expectations up front is important.

Rent control is great for tenants who benefit from it. But for landlords, there’s no such thing as cost control. Insurance, maintenance, and labor costs are all rising faster than inflation.

If a landlord doesn’t charge market rent, profit margins get squeezed. Mismanage the rent schedule long enough and the profits disappear, which is why some landlords pull their properties off the market altogether. See what's happening NYC.

My initial thinking was that I was testing the market in 2025, and I was satisfied with the result. As long as rent rises 2.5% a year, I should at least cover 80% of the rising cost of insurance and basic maintenance.

My tenants are also relatively young with plenty of options on their side. I don’t expect them to stay longer than five years. More realistically, three. With so much wealth coming their way, I would think they'd want to buy a property eventually, either in San Francisco or back in their hometown.

Remember, I expected my previous tenants to stay three years, and they left after 1.2 despite having a daughter in school.

So at the end of the day, I’m following the lease I drew up and signed. If my tenants are still there after their fourth year, I’ll reconsider whether to raise the rent to market.

Back to the original question. Should a tenant’s sudden wealth change anything?

Tenants strike it rich all the time. One buys a lottery ticket on a whim and hits for $20 million. Another’s startup gets acquired by Big Tech. Another inherits a fortune from a grandparent they visited twice. Another gets promoted to managing director and starts earning well over $1 million a year overnight.

Now flip it around. Tenants also get laid off, go through divorces, get sick, and watch their portfolios drop 40%. How many landlords voluntarily cut the rent when that happens? Not many.

You can’t have it both ways. If a tenant’s bad luck doesn’t lower the rent, their good luck shouldn’t raise it.

A lease is a promise about a house, not a royalty on your tenant’s life. If my tenants make $50,000 or $50 million this year, the rent schedule stays the same. That’s the whole point of putting it in writing.

There’s also a practical side. Tenants who come into money are more likely to buy a home than renew. Pressure them and you may only speed up their exit. One vacant month at $10,250 wipes out roughly eight months of my $1,250 discount.

When good tenants eventually leave, I’ll reset to market rent. Until then, my word is worth more than $15,000 a year.

My problem as a landlord is that I optimize for peace and harmony. A property manager would likely optimize for maximum profit. But I’m not about to give up 1 to 2 months of rent a year when I don’t have a day job and have been managing properties since 2005.

Despite my experience, I still find raising the rent deeply uncomfortable. I’ve written about how to raise the rent and extend a lease without feeling guilty. Clearly, I’m still a work in progress.

That discomfort is the main reason I hand over a three-year rent schedule up front to avoid any future awkwardness. When a new tenant’s enthusiasm is highest, they see the terms. If they agree, they sign with no surprises. If not, no big deal.

Even though the lease goes month-to-month after the first year and the schedule isn’t legally binding, honoring my word has paid off over 21+ years. Changing the terms on tenants after a year is not the path to harmony, even if it is my right to do so.

If your tenants have caused no disturbances, always paid on time, been honest about what they’ve broken, and paid to fix it, it’s simply not worth raising the rent to market if you’re still cash flow positive. More harmony means longer hold periods, which is generally better for building wealth.

For income-seeking investors, it's worth noting that rental property income is superior to dividend stock income. Unlike a company that pays a dividend, when a house pays you rent every month, its value doesn’t drop by a commensurate amount. Wear and tear is real, but it’s nothing like a dollar-for-dollar decline.

If rents are surging in your city, follow the lease and give your landlord zero excuses to raise the rent. To improve your odds further, send a small gift from time to time. Even a $25 gift goes a long way. It may sound ridiculous, but this kind of emotional intelligence can save you thousands of dollars.

Also, the more self-sufficient you are at fixing things and the less you contact your landlord, the more likely your rent stays reasonable. Besides, who wants to go back and forth with a landlord anyway?

Just know this leeway mostly exists with mom-and-pop landlords. A corporate landlord’s pricing software doesn’t care about your gift. A human landlord with a conscience might.

Readers, if your tenants suddenly struck it rich from an IPO, inheritance, or lottery win, would you raise the rent to market or honor your original terms? Should landlords cut the rent when tenants fall on hard times, if they’d raise it when tenants get rich? Do multi-year rent schedules make sense, or are they just leaving money on the table? And tenants, would you send your landlord a $25 gift to keep your rent down, or would that feel like a bribe?

If this post made you realize being a landlord means leaving money on the table, eating rising costs, and agonizing over rent increases, there’s another way to own real estate.

Check out Fundrise, my favorite private real estate investing platform. Instead of fixing toilets or negotiating leases, you can invest in a diversified portfolio of residential and industrial real estate, starting with as little as $10.

No midnight calls about leaky faucets or awkward rent conversations. No tenants striking it rich while you honor a three-year rent schedule. 100% passive instead.

I’ve personally invested with Fundrise, and they’ve been a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

#8439. Micro-Investing App Fees – $4 a Month Costs 9.6% a Year on $500

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

To see what a micro-investing app’s flat monthly fee costs you, multiply it by 12 and divide by your balance. On a small balance, that yearly percentage can be close to or above the 10% a year large U.S. stocks have averaged since 1928. Until it falls under 1%, invest through a broker with no account fee.

Acorns charges $4, $8, or $12 a month, depending on the plan, and Stash’s plan costs $12 a month, or $108 for a year paid up front. Those prices stay the same whatever your balance, so they take the biggest percentage of a small one.

At $4 a month, you pay $48 a year, which is 9.6% of a $500 balance. That 9.6% is nearly all of the 10% a year the S&P 500, an index of 500 large U.S. companies, has returned on average since 1928, according to data from NYU professor Aswath Damodaran.

Index stock mutual funds, which track an index like the S&P 500, charged an average fee of 0.05% a year in 2025, the Investment Company Institute found. On the same $500, that’s 25 cents a year against the app’s $48.

When you do the math, count every balance the fee covers, the app’s retirement account included, not just its regular investing account. A $12 monthly fee on $2,000 across both is $144 a year, or 7.2%.

Round-ups, which invest the spare change from each purchase, can be worth the fee while they’re the only way you’d invest at all. You can build the same habit for free, though. Check what your round-ups added last month, then set up an automatic monthly investment of that amount at an online broker with no account fee. Pick one that sells fractional shares, so even $20 buys a slice of a fund that tracks the S&P 500.

The fee drops below 1% a year, a tenth of the S&P 500’s 10% average, once your balance reaches 1,200 times the monthly fee. That’s a balance of $4,800 on a $4 plan and $14,400 on a $12 plan.

To set up that automatic investment, compare the best online brokers, or, to keep your round-ups, the best micro-investing apps.

#8438. Jordanian Man Trekking 23,000Km From South Africa to Siberia

Saddam Al Alaya is almost a year into his attempt to walk 23,000km from Cape Town, South Africa, to Magadan, in Russia’s Far East. The 35-year-old Jordanian left Cape Town on January 1, 2026, on a trek that he estimates will take three years. He covered the 5,500km to Rwanda in nine months, so he is on schedule.

This year, Al Alaya has already passed through South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Tanzania, Burundi, and now Rwanda. He expects to transit 18 countries in all, including his home country of Jordan, which he will cross from south to north.

Al Alaya grew up in Wadi Musa, beside Petra, and began guiding tourists around the famous archaeological site and the nearby canyons when he was about 16. He continued to guide while working for a business degree. He conceived the idea for this long walk in 2021, and spent almost five years organizing it.

Al Alaya meets a supporter. Photo: Facebook

Like so many adventurers, he wants to give his project a social angle, but Al Alaya seems particularly good at this. He founded an organization called Hike With Me, and many of his social media images show him glad-handing officials, walking with local people, or visiting regional schools. He often carries a white flag, symbolizing peace.

Al Alaya has official sponsorship from several Jordanian ministries, national organizations, and Jordanian embassies in various countries along the way. These have helped him with visas, security, and logistical support, according to the Jordanian News Agency.

#8437. In Your 50s, Max Your Catch-Up Contributions and Build a Bond Cushion

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

From the year you turn 50, catch-up rules let you add $8,000 a year to a 401(k) and $1,100 to an IRA beyond the regular limits. Raise your contributions to use them. Shift gradually toward bonds until a few years of retirement withdrawals sit in bonds and cash, so a crash can’t force you to sell stocks low.

Your 50s are the last decade when extra savings still have years to grow, and the first when a crash could hit just before you need the money.

The IRS’s catch-up rules stack the 401(k) catch-up on top of the regular limit of $24,500 a year. In the years you turn 60 through 63, the catch-up rises to $11,250 if your plan offers the higher amount. The IRA catch-up adds to the regular $7,500 limit.

At a hypothetical 6% annual return, an extra $8,000 a year in a 401(k) for the 10 years from age 55 to 65 grows to about $105,000.

To get the full catch-up, set your contribution rate to cover the regular limit plus the catch-up over the year. If your wages from your employer topped $150,000 last year, the catch-up has to go in as Roth money, taxed now instead of when you withdraw it. In that case, a plan with no Roth option can’t accept your catch-up at all.

Build the bond cushion gradually. Each year, move a little more of your savings from stocks to bonds, or send new contributions to bonds, rather than switching all at once. By your retirement date, aim to hold a few years of withdrawals in bonds and cash, since losses early in retirement do the most damage.

Start planning now, too, for when to claim Social Security and how you’ll pay for health insurance if you retire before Medicare begins at 65.

Raise your 401(k) contribution rate on your plan’s website before your next payday, since catch-ups come only out of paychecks and must go in before the plan year ends.

#8436. Bargiel Abandons Dhaulagiri Ski Attempt

Andrzej Bargiel and his team have also retreated from Dhaulagiri, citing bad weather and poor conditions. No one will summit Dhaulagiri this season.

Bargiel’s team, outfitted by Seven Summit Treks, reached Camp 2 while other climbing teams returned to Base Camp. The other teams turned back because of a lack of fixed ropes, and subsequently ended their expeditions.

But Bargiel still hoped to summit the peak and ski down to Base Camp. He planned to move up to Camp 3 yesterday and summit today, according to The Tourism Times. Bargiel did not share his exact location during the expedition, and his team often reported his progress with some delay. However, the skier reportedly retreated to Base Camp yesterday evening.

“Unfortunately, I had to give up on reaching the summit given the conditions we encountered,” Bargiel’s team quoted him saying. “Over the past few days, we’ve had significant snowfall accompanied by extremely strong, almost hurricane-force winds, and this created a high avalanche risk, which was the main reason I decided to turn back.”

This aligns with conditions described by the rope-fixing team last weekend, when they stopped work on the route. Soon after, commercial teams pushing for the summit were told to return to Base Camp.

“On a positive note, I had a great ski descent from Camp 2, with plenty of fresh snow. We’re all safe and heading home, and that’s what matters most,” Bargiel said.

The skier will not launch any further attempts this season to ski Dhaulagiri. Seven Summit Treks has officially closed the expedition with a rare statement explaining their decision to halt rope-fixing work. They cited their “guide’s decision” to turn around after assessing that conditions were not safe on the upper sections of the mountain.

The expedition’s director, Chhang Dawa Sherpa, was countering accusations by climbers that the rope-fixing team had lost their motivation after Seven Summit Treks’ biggest clients abandoned their summit attempts. You can read the full statement below:

This year, the highest point climbers reached on Dhaulagiri was around 7,100m, only slightly above Camp 3. No one has seen the conditions on the traverse below the summit ridge and the couloirs leading to the summit area.

Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er that no client summited this season, after a record number of teams halted their Manaslu attempts because of excess snow on the route. Only the rope fixers summited Manaslu. Two Russian climbers eyeing Makalu also decided to go home. With no permits issued yet for Kangchenjunga or Lhotse, the only summit chance on Nepal’s highest peaks now lies with the Russian team on Everest.

#8435. Cyclist Beats Pony Express Horseback Record

Lachlan Morton has completed a 3,217km bicycle journey along the historic Pony Express route from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California.

His time, 6 days, 21 hours, 15 minutes, beat the fastest recorded horseback mail relay from 1861 by 19 hours and 45 minutes.

Pony Express Trail. Photos: Top, Lachlan Morton/Instagram. Bottom: Shutterstock

Morton crossed eight states, negotiating remote desert tracks, the Great Basin and the Sierra Nevada. He encountered freezing conditions, fierce headwinds, and sections of barely discernible trail where he had to push his bicycle.

Unlike the original Pony Express, which changed riders and horses, Morton cycled the entire distance himself. However, he used different bicycles and had a support vehicle carrying supplies.

Morton is an Australian professional cyclist whose career spans elite road racing, gravel competition, and ultra-endurance adventure cycling. Rather than focusing solely on traditional racing, he has become widely recognized for long-distance challenges.

#8434. Wildfires Force Closure of Carstenz Pyramid for the Season

All around the world, natural disasters are hampering climbing expeditions. The latest case is a series of uncontrolled wildfires in Papua that have doomed the fall climbing season on Carstenz Pyramid.

The region is facing severe, widespread forest fires that have blanketed the island in a persistent thick haze. The air quality and visibility have reached levels that make transportation, logistics, and climbing operations impossible, according to local outfitter Tropic Adventure Papua. Apparently, the effects of the El Niño phenomenon, known this year as the Super Niño due to its extraordinary intensity, are to blame. It has brought a prolonged drought and extremely dry air, diminishing hope for the rain needed to extinguish the fires.

By the time the situation became unbearable, the first groups of foreign climbers had reached Timika in Papua, but no one made it to the top during this season, which is now officially canceled.

Outfitters have already shared the news with their clients and are now placing their hopes in 2027.

“Our thoughts are with the local communities affected, and we’re hoping the fires are brought under control soon,” Garrett Madison posted on social media. Instead, they have set the dates for next year, with two trips in March and October.

Tragically, the situation in Papua is only a fraction of a major environmental catastrophe. Wildfires are sweeping through the Indonesian archipelago and affecting Malaysia and Singapore:

The harm caused to the fragile Indonesian ecosystem is incalculable. In recent days, a viral video of a young orangutan rescued from a treetop where it tried to escape with burned hands and feet has drawn attention to the disaster. In fact, a significant number of primates were evacuated by rescue services in Borneo. Some of them were returned to the forests as the fire receded last weekend, according to the BBC.

The intensity of the fires in Papua and the air quality can be tracked live here.

At 4,884m, Carstenz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya in the local language) is the highest point of Oceania and considered one of the Seven Summits. Located in Central Papua, and with a tropical climate, Carstenz can be climbed at any time of year. However, summit options increase in the less rainy months, from February through November.

Outfitters apply for permits twice a year. Political unrest has often kept climbers away in the past, and major mining operations limit ground access. Climbers are typically airlifted to Base Camp instead of trekking through the jungle.

#8433. Russians Give Up on the Khumbu Icefall; Will Try Everest West Ridge Instead

The first steps on a lonely Everest were daunting for four Russian climbers, who tried and failed to cross the Khumbu Icefall. They adapted quickly, heading up to the Lho La instead and setting up camp at that high pass at the base of the West Ridge.

Andrei Vasiliev, Natalya Belyankina, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Valery Sipilov set off from Lobuche on their first round up the mountain last week. Their original plan was to attempt the Khumbu Icefall, which has no ladders or ropes at this time of year. They set off at 5 am on October 9, looking for a way through the maze of seracs and crevasses.

“At first glance, it appears to be pure, unadulterated chaos,” Sergey Kondrashkin later wrote. “Yet on closer inspection, one can discern distinct sections. We opted for the central section, which seemed somewhat more solid — though ‘solid is a relative term…At least, it was easier to envision a viable path here between the seracs, snowfields, and ice walls.”

The recent snowy spell that hit Nepal filled many of the crevasses but also had a downside: loads of hard trail-breaking through deep snow.

Kondrashkin reported they crossed the most difficult terrain with only a few ropes in some sections and mostly moved as a roped team of four. “Time and again, I broke through the surface, sinking in up to my waist or even my chest,” he wrote. “By the end of the day, we reached an altitude of 5,700m, with still 500 vertical meters to go to the top of the Icefall and the biggest crevasses on the upper part.” They planted their tent on a small, flat platform.

“Conditions did not improve on the following morning,” Natalya Belyankina reported. “We ran out of steam on the second day, having gained only 100m in elevation after six hours, so we decided to head back down.”

The Russian team in the Khumbu Icefall on Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

However, they had food for four days, so instead of returning to Lobuche, they retraced their steps across the Icefall in three hours (they had spent one day and a half going up) and pitched the tent right below the high pass known as Lho La.

That was their second potential route. The Lho La is the col between Khumbutse, a lesser peak that rises to the left, and the characteristic pyramidal peak known as Everest’s West Shoulder. Lying on the border between Nepal and Tibet, it gives access to the very long West Ridge to the summit. It is also the route that Jost Kobusch will attempt in two months’ time. The German is on his fourth attempt to solo Everest in winter.

The Russian team’s tent in front of the wall leading to the Lho La between Nepal and Tibet. Photo: Natalya Belyankina/Instagram

Progress up the Lho La was fast, unlike the Icefall. The team completed the mixed terrain of the 600m wall in a single day, then pitched their tent on the col. On the fourth day, they scouted the terrain above and went to the base of the West Ridge, before returning to Lobuche for now, Alpymon reported.

The Russian team on a lonely Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

The climbers loved the experience of being completely alone on Everest. “Groups of trekkers only make it as far as that famous rock — joking, laughing, and congratulating one another,” Belyankina recalled. “Just yesterday, near the Everest Base Camp rock, a young man was playing the saxophone. It sounded wonderful. But once we cross a couple of moraines, that’s it — we’re all alone on the mountain.”

#8432. Google’s Collapse Gives Hope for the Middle Class and Our Kids

I’ve been a Google shareholder since 2010 and I'm thankful. But yesterday’s earnings, and the 12% collapse that followed, left me thoroughly disappointed.

Search is under siege. Gemini isn’t leading the AI race. And Google is spending like a drunken sailor to catch up.

Spending $200 billion in CAPEX is more than the GDP of most countries. And free cash flow just went negative $9 billion for the quarter.

What does $200 billion buy you? Third or fourth place in the AI race, depending on who you ask. Behind Anthropic. Behind OpenAI. Maybe neck and neck with whoever else is closing fast.

That’s pathetic. And as a shareholder, it’s demoralizing. Not even Berkshire Hathaway investing $10 billion at $350/share can save us.

Google researchers wrote the 2017 paper that introduced the transformer, the “T” in ChatGPT. Google owns DeepMind. It designs its own TPU chips. It has Search, YouTube, Android, Gmail, and roughly 3 billion Chrome users. It understood large language models years before most of us knew what it was.

And yet most developers aren’t coding with Gemini. They’re using Claude Code, Codex, or something else.

In the most transformational technology since the internet went mainstream, Google had a ten-mile head start, outspent nearly everyone, and still got lapped.

Meanwhile, executives collected enormous pay packages. Nice work, which most of us can't get.

Everybody in the Bay Area knows Google is one of the best places to “rest and vest.” HBO’s Silicon Valley spoofed it with Big Head, who got promoted at Hooli into a big title, a rooftop office, and zero responsibilities.

Who doesn’t want to get paid a lot to work less? Of course there are plenty of hard-working people at Google.

But resting and vesting only feels good when the stock keeps going up. When the stock stalls, you’re just resting and asking whether this is all there is to life.

I’ve seen this movie before. I left Credit Suisse in 2012 partly because technology was squeezing the business. Algorithmic trading was compressing commissions toward zero, which is why trading is basically free today.

Our Asian equities group was competitive. But the firm overall was lagging Goldman, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and UBS. Staying at a firm falling behind, in an industry being hollowed out, felt like polishing brass on a sinking ship.

So I left to build my own thing. I made a fraction of my old income for years. But watching something I built actually grow was more thrilling than any bonus check.

Momentum is energizing. Decline is a slow poison, even when the paycheck clears.

Part of the reason I invested in Google was its dominance. Two Stanford PhD students, who fittingly never finished their PhDs, hired an army of brilliant nerds from Stanford, MIT, and the Indian Institute of Technology.

They commanded over 90% search market share. They piled up over $100 billion in cash. Then they used monopoly profits to enter new businesses and crush the competition.

In other words, Google became the trust fund kid. Let’s call him Chip.

Chip was born on third base. Parent's money, the search monopoly, pays for everything. Grandpa’s name is on the library, which is the transformer paper and DeepMind. Family friends can make one phone call and open any door, which is Android, Chrome, and the default search deal with Apple.

Chip still posts on Instagram about his “grind” while sipping a $28 smoothie.

Everybody else in the AI race is the middle-class or poor kid. There is no way Chip should lose his incredible head start, unless he really messes up.

OK, maybe I’m being a little extreme. OpenAI has Microsoft’s money. Anthropic has Amazon’s money. Their founders went to Princeton, Stanford, and other elite schools. Nobody here is eating ramen.

But wealth is relative. If everybody is a millionaire, nobody is rich. Next to Google, everybody is middle class.

Google started the AI race with billions of users, a cash machine, and its own chips. Everyone else started with zero users and had to beg investors for money just to rent compute. Every dollar they raised came with a pitch deck and a deadline.

The middle-class kid has to justify every dollar. The trust fund kid just asks Dad for $200 billion.

And here’s the most trust fund kid thing of all. Google is an investor in Anthropic. Chip is literally paying tuition for the kid who’s beating him.

As a capitalist, you usually don’t bet against Chip when he’s smart and connected. You invest in him. I’ve watched the kid with every advantage win since 2004, when Google went public.

But every so often, Chip gets comfortable. He takes a third gap year. He hires expensive consultants to tell him what he should already know. Shiny object syndrome takes hold, and financial resources and attention get diverted to solving core problems.

Meanwhile, the middle-class kid has no safety net. If he doesn’t ship, he doesn’t eat.

Dario Amodei is a good example. He grew up middle class in San Francisco. His dad was a leather craftsman. His mom managed library projects. He went to Lowell, a public high school, studied hard, and actually finished his PhD.

In 2021, he co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela and a group of colleagues. Five years later, Claude is what developers reach for, and Anthropic is one of the most valuable private companies on earth.

It’s Google versus the world. And the world is the rest of us.

The trust fund kid has every advantage except one. He doesn’t need to win.

The middle-class kid has only one advantage. He must win or be relegated to the permanent underclass.

Hunger is the great equalizer. And unlike a trust fund, it can’t be inherited.

There’s another reason I’m not shedding too many tears for Chip, even though my portfolio needs to go to the ER. For years, he’s been taking other people’s lunch money.

Google built its empire by sending traffic to websites like mine. That was the deal. Bloggers, journalists, and small publishers created the content. Google organized it, sold ads around it, and sent readers our way. Everybody ate.

First came featured snippets, which lifted our answers onto the results page so readers didn’t need to click. Then Google stuffed its own products at the top: shopping results, travel results, maps, “People also ask” boxes, and more ads. The organic results, the content people actually searched for, got pushed so far down you needed a scuba tank to find them.

Then came AI Overviews. Now Google reads our work, summarizes it, and serves it as its own answer at the top of the page. The attribution, if there is any, is a tiny link most people never click.

Imagine writing from firsthand experience since 2009, only to watch a multi-trillion-dollar company repackage your insights and keep the reader. That’s not a search engine. That’s a very polite pickpocket.

And yes, I know the AI companies trained on publishers’ work too without attribution or payment. You have to steal people’s work to get rich sometimes. Nobody in this race has clean hands. But Google was supposed to be the partner. It sent us traffic for two decades before deciding it would rather keep it. So now it stomps on us too.

I don’t want to oversell the hope. Since graduating college in 1999, I’ve watched the rich get far richer than everybody else.

The first reason is math. The rich have more capital, so a bull market hands them bigger absolute dollar gains. The longer compounding runs, the bigger the pile gets.

I saw it at Goldman in NYC, at Credit Suisse in SF, and every year since I left in 2012. Some friends from my tennis club who were mere millionaires 15 years ago are now multi-billionaires.

The second reason is proximity. Rich people mostly hang out with other rich people. And proximity creates opportunity.

Once you’re an LP, you might get invited to co-invest in a hot private AI company the fund has high conviction in. That’s how the gap widens, one quiet invitation at a time. Be nice and helpful to as many people as possible.

Everybody rolls their eyes at networking. I hated it too. It’s likely the main reason I never made Managing Director. I couldn’t fake enough agreeableness with the powers that be.

The lesson to pass to our kids: you don’t have to be fake. But you do have to show up and always play nice with others if you want to get ahead

The beauty of FIRE is freedom. The problem with being a FIRE parent is that your network withers once you leave the workforce.

The people who could introduce you to clients, write a preschool recommendation letter, or refer you for a better job slowly disappear. And if you’re truly FIRE, you stop caring about getting ahead. Otherwise you’d still be trading time for money.

Then you have kids. And suddenly, money and status matter again in a hurry.

That’s why Google’s stumble actually provides hope, despite the paper loss.

If a company with $100 billion in cash, 3 billion users, the transformer itself, and a $200 billion annual budget can fumble its lead, then advantages aren’t destiny. They’re a head start. And head starts can be squandered.

Which means a hungry kid with no connections still has a real shot. So does the poorest minority kid in America.

My children won’t inherit a monopoly. But they can inherit a work ethic, some hunger, and the knowledge that Chip can be beaten.

Look, you’ve had a great run. Thank you for your hard work all these years. Google’s strategic drift isn’t your fault. That’s on the C-suite.

But as a shareholder, I have two requests.

This is wartime, not peacetime. Mass layoffs are likely coming, and the people who survive them tend to be the ones who are visibly in the building.

It’s been fun playing pickleball with many of you at 11:30 a.m. on a Tuesday. I’ll miss the competition. But that has to stop now.

The stock could be dead money for a year or two while the supertanker turns. If you’re only staying for the next vest, you’re not resting. You’re rotting.

Golden handcuffs are still handcuffs. And gold is heavy.

Go be the middle-class kid again in your own career. Join or start something where you have to win. That’s what Jeff Dean and colleagues did with the launch of Discovery Loop.

What doesn’t work is the middle path: staying, coasting, and feeling empty. That’s the worst of both worlds for you and for us shareholders. If you decide to leave, please try to negotiate a severance package. You have nothing to lose.

Google has the resources to recover. Trust fund kids usually get a second or third chance. The only question is whether Chip still wants it badly enough. It’s hard when you’re already so rich.

Readers, do you think Google can regain its AI lead, or has the trust fund kid permanently lost his edge? Is spending $200 billion a year a sign of strength or desperation? If you work at a big tech company, are you resting and vesting, or quietly planning your exit? And as a parent, how are you teaching your kids to compete without a trust fund or a powerful network?
