#8413. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

First Highline on Trango Tower: On August 17, Lukas Irmler and Antonia Ruede-Passul of Germany completed the first-ever highline walk on Trango Towers in Pakistan’s Karakoram. They climbed Great Trango Tower to acclimatize before tackling Nameless Tower.

Setting up the 21m highline required fixed ropes and two summit ascents of Nameless Tower. The successful crossing saw Ruede-Passul break her own women’s highline altitude world record, previously set at 5,860m on Ojos de Salado in Chile, while Irmler surpassed 6,000m for the first time.

Following in the footsteps of Norway’s Great Adventurers: Steffen Skjottelvik set out to cross Canada, by foot, dog sled, and canoe, accompanied only by his beloved sled dogs. The Norwegian began his journey in 2023, but when one dog fell ill, he paused in the remote Cree community of Peawanuck. Here he found his home and a way of life that fitted him perfectly. He also fell in love with a local woman and became a second son to the community elders.

His original plan to travel by sled across the Hudson Bay coast changed after wolves killed one of his lead dogs. He decided to canoe the coastline in summer instead.

In 2025, he set off with his malamute Togo and a husky named Bay, facing polar bears, powerful tides, dense bogs, clouds of biting flies, and river crossings. On August 15, exhausted after weeks of difficult travel, Steffen could finally see his endpoint — the town of York Factory across the Hayes River. All he had to do was cross it. Togo survived and made it to shore, but Steffen’s body was found downstream 10 days later.

Where Was ‘Tenzing’ Filmed? Apple TV’s Tenzing recreates the historic 1953 first ascent of Everest, this time with Sherpa Tenzing Norgay at the center of the story. The filmmakers used real alpine environments across Nepal and New Zealand rather than green screens.

Nepal provided locations for Tenzing’s early life in the Lower Mustang, as well as the scenes in Darjeeling, Kathmandu, and Everest Base Camp. New Zealand’s Southern Alps, particularly the Aoraki region, doubled for Everest’s glaciers and icefalls, with the Darwin Icefall standing in for the notorious Khumbu Icefall.

Photographer Encounters Magnificent White Stag: Wildlife photographer Brian Johnston has captured incredible images of a rare white stag, believed to be an albino red deer. Johnston and a friend spotted the stag one windy morning during the rutting season, but it detected them and ran off.

Returning the following day, they found it asleep in a field, apparently exhausted after a night of rutting activity. Eventually, it stood up, giving Johnston the opportunity to photograph it.

Shark Attack Survivor Recounts Losing His Leg While Surfing: Australian firefighter and surfer Mel Ismail was surfing at Glenfield Beach on Australia’s west coast on September 14, when he was attacked by a shark. Sitting beyond the breaking waves, watching a pod of dolphins, Ismail initially thought a dolphin had bumped into his leg. Suddenly, he was dragged underwater and realized what was happening.

He desperately tried to push his fingers into the shark’s large black eye, and it released him. Ismail was bleeding heavily but managed to catch a wave toward shore. Another surfer spotted him and helped him onto the beach. Despite losing his leg below the knee, Ismail is determined to return to the water and start bodyboarding as soon as he can.

Canoe Dig It: Sam Dunning discovered freestyle canoeing during the 2020 lockdown after seeing a video of master paddler Marc Ornstein performing an interpretive routine to music. Amazed by the combination of technical skill and on-water choreography, the New York-based actor and filmmaker began writing Canoe Dig It?, a mockumentary inspired by comedies such as This Is Spinal Tap.

Winning the paddling community’s support was not easy, but at a freestyle canoeing symposium in Ohio, Dunning eventually met Ornstein. Ornstein and his wife agreed to be stunt doubles for the film.

Into Thin Air: This is a good background to the stories we’ve done on Kalie McCrystal, the 38-year-old skyrunner who disappeared on the Matterhorn on September 1. She met a Polish climber on her ascent, and theirs is the last footage of her. It shows her climbing towards the 4,478m summit. Shortly afterward, she was spotted descending the Italian side. Then she vanished.

Mountain rescuers believe she fell between 4,100m and 4,250m, but cannot establish exactly where or in which direction she fell. Despite a thorough search, no clothing, blood, or remains have been found. Her mother and sister eventually accepted that she had died on the mountain.

Climber Awarded Carnegie Medal After Rescuing Hang Glider Pilot: Matthew Clark has been awarded the Carnegie Medal for rescuing a hang glider pilot who crashed into a cliff on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

Clark, a 24-year-old climber and paraglider, had launched from the same spot minutes apart. Clark had just landed when he heard the crash reported over his radio. Reaching the scene with other pilots, he found Parson suspended in his harness around 15m above the ground.

With no walkable route to him, Clark spotted a narrow chimney nearby and free soloed up it, reaching him in about five minutes. Clark cut Parson free, moved him to safer ground, dressed a gash on his knee, and waited with him until a helicopter team was able to extract him on a long line.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8412. How To Keep Your Middle Class Membership Card

The middle class is the best class in the world. It is the largest class, which means it’s the most important class. Politicians pander to us by saying nice things and giving us all sorts of random benefits, like the child tax credit or stimulus checks if you make a middle-class income.

But once you get to the upper middle class, or the mass affluent class, those government benefits start going away. You make more than the middle class, but not enough more to avoid the sting of higher taxes and optional lifestyle choices, like paying for private school. And because you make more than the middle class, you are sometimes vilified.

If you need proof of the middle class’s power, look no further than this week’s midterms. Democrats just won both the House and the Senate.

The middle class is fed up with extremely wealthy politicians who provide tax breaks for their wealthy friends who don’t need them. Fed up with 28-year-old AI researchers buying $8 million homes in cash while their product threatens humanity’s existence. Fed up with high gas prices, high mortgage rates, a never-ending war, and a grocery bill that looks like a car payment.

When the largest class in America gets angry, it doesn’t write a strongly worded email. It votes. And it flips Congress.

The lesson is clear. If you want politicians to care about you, be middle class. If you want them to tax you, be rich. And if you want to be ignored and vilified at the same time, be upper middle class.

This is where we find ourselves with today’s post on how to be middle class and stay middle class, so you can feel safe, loved, and accepted.

Because based on the feedback from 3.5 million views and 1,400+ comments on X for my $408,000 budget post, I now clearly understand what is and isn’t allowed if you want to keep your middle class membership card.

So you think earning $408,000 a year is a lot of money? After working 50+ hours a week, being stressed out of your mind, and barely seeing your kids, it might not be the dream income you imagined.Look how quickly the money goes. $1/month left over.What would you cut? pic.twitter.com/AFGYHEdeQG

One of the biggest surprises from all the feedback on the $408,000 budget was that three weeks of vacation a year, two destination trips and one staycation, is considered an absurd luxury. The vast majority of commenters called it out of touch, ludicrous, or worse.

There was even a writer with 1.5 million Twitter followers who said he's never taken more than two weeks off in his life. He later explained it's because he doesn't make enough to take three weeks off. So if you needed more proof that writing doesn't pay, there it is.

Since 2009, I've considered three weeks of vacation a year the standard for anyone with a decade-plus of experience. This is a household making $408,000 with two kids. These aren't people fresh out of college. Taking 0-1 weeks in your first year or three, sure, that tracks. But after 10+ years in the workforce, three weeks off is not some wild ask.

Apparently it is. So the rule stands corrected: if you want to be middle class, cap your vacation at two weeks a year. Take a third week and you've officially graduated to out-of-touch elite. Congratulations, or condolences.

Not one of the 1,400 commenters gave this household credit for driving a paid-off Honda CR-V. A brand new, nicely equipped CR-V runs about $38,000, compared to roughly $50,000 for the average new car in America today.

So the verdict is in: the middle class are free, encouraged even, to spend more than they should on a car. This household is decidedly not following my 1/10th rule for car buying, the way personal finance nerds, the mass affluent, the rich, or the poor do.

Ironically, the nicer the car someone drives, up to a point, the more middle class they appear. It's understood that the middle class take on debt, or at least stretch, for a car nicer than their income comfortably supports. That's the badge. Wear it proudly, on 72-month financing.

There was a genuine uproar about this household paying $5,000/month for their mortgage. If you live in an expensive coastal city, $5,000 is reasonable, maybe even cheap, for a single-family home. But the feedback was clear: $5,000 is too much, and so is 2,100 square feet.

Three bedrooms and two bathrooms still reads as the quintessential middle class home to me, and I'll defend that. What's apparently not middle class is the 2,100 square feet of interior space. Plenty of commenters flagged that as immodest and far too big.

So if you want to keep your middle class card, buy or rent something under 2,000 square feet. Ideally something starting with a 1: 1,600, 1,800, even 1,990 sqft works. Just don't let that second digit round up to a 2.

With a modest home and an expensive car, this household also isn't following my House-To-Car Ratio guide either. The typical American runs a ratio of about 9 to 15. I recommend readers aim for at least 50, ideally 100+, so you're minimizing a depreciating liability while maximizing an appreciating asset. The middle class, evidently, prefer it the other way around.

Since a huge amount of education is now available for free online, paying for grade school is an unnecessary luxury the middle class shouldn't indulge in. Same logic applies to paying full freight for private or public university.

A smart, motivated kid with engaged parents will likely do fine in almost any academic setting. So dropping serious money on private grade school tuition is, by this logic, mostly a waste. Save and then invest it so the tuition money grows to over $1 million by the time they graduate college.

Then again, having over $1 million to give your 23-year-old college graduate because you saved and invested the difference disqualifies you from being middle class. So instead of saving and investing the difference, feel free to spend it on whatever your heart desires. YOLO!

Of course this household earns their $408,000 the hardest way possible: two W2 salaries, taxed at near the top of the marginal bracket before a single dollar hits their checking account. Federal, state, FICA, all of it withheld before they ever see it.

Nobody in the comments seemed bothered by this part. And that's the tell. The middle class don't just tolerate a W2 job, they build an identity around it. Steady paycheck, steady withholding, steady sense that this is simply how adults earn money.

Ask them about starting something of their own, a side business, a rental, an app, anything with equity attached, and the answer is almost always the same: too risky. Better to let somebody else take the risk, and the upside, while you collect a salary and help build their dream instead of your own.

Entrepreneurship isn't guaranteed. But neither is a W2 job in a layoff cycle. The middle class would rather have the certainty of somebody else's risk than the upside of their own.

If you're a working middle class professional, the going rate is two kids, maybe. Every additional kid means more daycare, more food, more square footage you're apparently not supposed to have, and no extra help from the government to offset any of it.

But stop working, or work little enough to qualify for subsidies, and suddenly more children becomes affordable again. Medicaid, subsidized childcare, food assistance, the EITC, all of it scales with need, not with effort.

The system isn't rewarding family size. It's rewarding low reported income, and if you're grinding away at a W2 job trying to move up, you're the one least likely to qualify for help raising the family you're working so hard to support.

So the rule holds. Two working parents, two kids, tops. Three kids or more puts you in the rich category. The middle class don’t have what some call trophy kids given it can take a fortune to raise them.

Curiously, there was a lot of pushback about the $408,000 household saving $16,000 a year for their two children's college tuition. Commenters asked why they'd bother saving for college when they're already paying $45,000 a year for private grade school per kid.

My initial response was that college can be far more expensive than $45,000 a year. Some universities now cost $100,000 to $120,000 a year, all-in. So setting aside additional money for college isn't a bad idea. But critics said the parents should just pay for college out of their day job income when the time comes.

Therefore, the middle class do not proactively save and invest for college in tax-advantaged 529 plans. And given many top private universities now charge $0 tuition for households earning under $200,000 a year, the belief that saving for college is unnecessary is, in fairness, somewhat logical.

What's illogical is assuming your kid has a real shot at one of these schools with a sub-7% acceptance rate. But the middle class are hopeful their children will defy the odds when such schools cater predominantly to the rich.

As an older parent, it never occurred to me not to save for college, because I don't plan on working to pay for it when the time comes. When my youngest goes to college, I'll be 61. There's no way I want to be grinding from 61 to 64, paying tuition, as someone who left the workforce in 2012. So the only way for me to pay for college is to save and build passive income.

Therefore, it's clear the middle class don't focus on building passive income through a taxable brokerage account, a rental property portfolio, or other taxable investments. The middle class are solely focused on contributing to tax-advantaged retirement accounts like the 401(k), IRA, and Roth IRA, which is great, until you actually want to stop working before 59 and a half.

Having the grit to work forever, whether you want to or not, is truly a wonderful trait of the middle class. It makes employers proud.

If any of this sounds absurd, that's the point. We judge other people's money and choices against our own experience, then call the mismatch a moral failing.

Personally, I love being part of the middle class, because nobody bothers you if you're like most people. But this exercise made me realize I've been too frugal in FIRE. I also need to build more grit by mentally preparing to work longer while spending more as a reward. So I'll do those things to retain my middle class membership card.

The $408,000 family isn't doing anything wrong. They're just the latest Rorschach test for what the internet has decided “middle class” is allowed to look like. We shouldn’t ignore the opinions of the 3.5 million viewers and 1,400+ commenters.

And if working until 70 because you never built passive income is the price of admission, then welcome to the club. Just make sure to invest some money in our overlords to avoid being part of the permanent underclass. Now that would be unacceptable.

Readers, do you agree with my conditions and descriptions of what makes someone middle class? What are some other conditions you might add?

If you want an actual framework for these decisions, car versus house, rent versus buy, private school versus public, W2 versus building your own thing, instead of a crowdsourced vibe check, that's what I wrote Buy This Not That for. It walks through the exact tradeoffs above (the 1/10th car rule, the House-To-Car Ratio) without the 1,400 comments telling you you're doing it wrong either way.

Sign up for the private Financial Samurai newsletter!

Sign up for the private Financial Samurai newsletter!

#8410. Here’s What All Hunters Should Know About the Rut, Weather, and Deer Movement, According to One of the Top Experts In the Country

Published Oct 29, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

During the whitetail pre-rut and rut, hunters should worry less about the type of weather that will “get deer moving” and focus more on weather conditions that will help us hunt more effectively. That’s one of my takeaways from interviewing Dr. Grant Woods, a renowned wildlife researcher and diehard deer hunter. Woods and his crew publish excellent informational hunting content on his website, Growing Deer TV.

I interviewed him on Halloween just as a spectacular cold front was sinking into the heart of deer country. But if you didn’t kill your target buck during that front, don’t worry. The hunting is still getting better, Woods says. You can listen to my full interview with Woods in the podcast episode below. And read on to learn Woods’ other tips for understanding the rut, weather, and deer activity.

Recent research has found that fronts, even big cold fronts like we just experienced, don’t increase whitetail rutting activity, Woods says.

“The research says that weather is not much of a [factor in regards to deer rutting activity],” he says. “And that’s caused a bit of an issue in the last few years between hunters and researchers in a lot of online chatter.”

This discrepancy stems from the fact that hunters tend to see more deer when cold fronts hit. So, what gives? Woods’ explanation is essentially that both researchers and hunters are right. Cold temps don’t speed up breeding activity, but they do mean that hunters are more likely to see deer from their stands.

“I’m going to tell you, during our cold front, we went from high 70s to 30 and under in 24 hours. And on my trail cameras, when that cold front hit, I got a big spike… So what I’m saying is there’s some miscommunication going on,” Woods says. “Putting my scientist hat on now, typically I can’t publish something unless … 95 times out of 100 it’s going to happen. Well there’s a lot of conflicting things [concerning weather and deer activity]. When did the barometer rise? How much of a temperature was it? What phase of the rut was it? There’s a lot of noise. And when there’s a lot of noise a good biologist that’s doing really good work is going to say ‘I can’t say X because there’s too much noise.’ They’re going to be a little more conservative if they’re doing honest science.”

So what’s the takeaway for the hunter? It’s important to know that in the pre-rut deer usually don’t go running far outside their home range, even on a big cold front. However, they might walk around more within their home range.

Also, it’s important to understand what the pre-rut really is. Woods defines the pre-rut as the time period during which less than 25 percent of does are receptive. Bucks are seeking or moving more. Every day, a few more does become receptive and that brings a frenzy to the bucks. All of this happens regardless of weather.

Read Next: The Best Cellular Trail Cameras: The Complete Guide to Cell Cams and Subscription Plans

Yep, deer will keep on rutting even when the weather warms.

“The rut is a bell shaped curve and we’re definitively climbing up that curve [right now]. We’re increasing in intensity. So even if it’s 80 degrees, but the prom only happens once where you hunt, it’s still going to happen [during a warm front],” Woods says. “Now hunters sometimes debate that but if you look [at spring fawning season], fawns are born at the same time in the same place every year. There’s going to be some early fawns, a big cluster of fawns, and then some late fawns. [That’s because] especially up North, if they’re born too early, they’re going to fall into a snowbank and they’re not going to make it. And if they’re born too late they’re not going to gain enough weight before the next winter and they’re not going to make it. So the system is pretty refined over a long time. The rut is going to happen at the same time [locally, every year].”

Most deer hunters love to focus on the big fronts, but small changes in temperature can make for productive hunting, too. Woods uses a rough temperature change rule when deciding when to hunt vs. when to work.

“When it’s been warmer than normal, I get excited when there’s a 10 percent temperature decrease.”

So if it’s been 80 degrees and the forecast is calling for a drop down to 72 degrees, Woods will plan on hunting. During the late season, when deer are moving during warmer periods, Woods will hunt during a 10 percent increase in temperature. That means a small bump, like from 30 to 33 degrees.

When the rut is increasing in intensity, like it is right now, typical and stable weather makes for great hunting days, too, Woods says.

If the conditions are hot and not favorable, it’s probably not the time to skip work for an all-day sit. But Woods suggests making a short evening hunt and sliding in closer to bedding areas (assuming you can do so without bumping deer). This is because deer are likely to move only a few minutes before the end of legal shooting light during hot days. So there’s a chance you could catch a buck just leaving his bed at the end of the day.

Don’t be fooled by that one trail camera photo of a buck you have moving during a rainstorm. Bucks actually tend to move less during a steady rain.

“Researchers, again using GPS collared deer, have seen that bucks tend to move less when it’s raining,” Woods says. He thinks this could be because they have a harder time detecting predators in the rain, with blowing leaves and other disturbances in the woods.

Strangely, however, does tend to move a little bit more in the rain, Woods says. No one is quite sure why.

Instead of worrying about how weather impacts deer, hunters should consider how weather affects our potential success as predators. Woods mentions barometric pressure as a good example. During high pressure and low humidity, hunters tend to see more deer. But that’s not necessarily because deer are moving more on high-pressure days (data say they don’t). Instead, it’s likely because high pressure days favor the hunter so we’re not getting busted by deer.

“On high-pressure days, our scent is actually rising. So we’re able to get closer to deer without them detecting our scent,” Wood says. “We’re not talking [enough] about a hunter’s ability to hunt. We’re totally focused on the deer and what’s making them move. We need to accept that they’re feeding and drinking and avoiding predators every day of their lives.”

“I don’t have any data on this, but understanding the science and being a diehard hunter, I believe the biggest problem is that we often don’t include the human element and we are alerting way more deer than we think we are.”

Read Next: The 101 Best Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

Wind is the biggest factor in our ability to hunt whitetails effectively—we all know this. But Woods says to analyze not just wind direction, but also wind speed and consistency. Hunters have the advantage during a strong (but not gusting) wind that is consistent in direction and speed.

This is one of the reasons why hunters tend to have success during cold fronts, Woods says. He suggests using NOAA’s Wind Roses page, which shows predominant wind direction and wind strength. This will help you get a better idea of how to set stands in your area.

Considering that deer live by their noses, Woods has a logical theory about why deer are most active at dawn and dusk. The temperature changes during morning (warming) and evening (cooling), often cause the wind to shift and swirl. A swirling wind helps deer detect predators from all directions, which makes them feel safer while moving and feeding.

“At night and full daytime deer only get nasal protection, if you will, from about 180 degrees —just throwing a number out,” Woods says. “But at sunrise and sunset, because the Earth is warming the Earth is cooling, thermals are shifting, they’re getting protection from a much greater area.”

One tactic Woods employs is executing very short hunts in the evening. The less time you’re out there, the less time there is for your scent to disperse and for that big buck to potentially bust you. —A.R.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8409. Forgotten 7,000'ers: Changtse

Changtse is a rarely climbed peak in Tibet in the Everest massif, flanked by the Main Rongbuk and East Rongbuk Glaciers, and linked to the world’s highest mountain by the North Col. With a prominence of only 497m, Changtse is subordinate to its parent peak.

Modern Chinese mapping lists Changtse at 7,543m, though older sources cite figures up to 7,583m. The Changtse Glacier flows north into the East Rongbuk system, and some geographic surveys note a glacial lake on the glacier near 6,216m, ranking it among the world’s highest.

Because of Changtse’s connection to the classic northern approach to Everest, early mountaineering parties repeatedly crossed its flanks long before treating it as an independent objective.

In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine became the first climbers to set foot on Changtse. They climbed the East Ridge while scouting camp locations during the British Everest expedition.

During the 1935 British Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition led by Eric Shipton, the team divided to scout possible climbs before targeting Changtse. Bill Tilman and Edmund Wigram considered the peak’s Northwest Ridge but deemed it impracticable and crossed north of Changtse to Camp 2.

Meanwhile, Michael Spender and Charles Warren established high-altitude survey stations, and Shipton and Dan Bryant explored the West Rongbuk Glacier. Shipton’s primary goals were to photograph Everest’s upper sections and gather data on monsoon snow behavior. Despite deteriorating weather and waist-deep snow, they established three high camps.

On August 21, 1935, Shipton, Tilman, Wigram, Bryant, and Warren launched an attempt on Changtse. They climbed to within 460m of the summit before dangerously deep, soft monsoon snow forced them back. They spent a freezing night at high camp. Then, confronted by unstable slopes and buried tents, they abandoned their summit attempt.

Moving down the East Rongbuk Glacier on August 23, the climbers reunited with Spender, who had completed his difficult survey work, and headed toward the Kharta Changri Pass.

Base Camp of the 1924 Everest expedition. Photo: Royal Geographic Society

In 1952, during the British Cho Oyu Expedition, Edmund Hillary, George Lowe, and three Sherpas illegally crossed the Nup La Pass into Chinese-controlled Tibet after abandoning their Cho Oyu climb.

The group traveled to the North Side of Everest, exploring the East Rongbuk Glacier and visiting pre-war British base camp sites. Subsequently, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier for a direct attempt on Changtse’s summit. They reached 6,600m before a lack of food and supplies forced them to turn back. They returned over the pass to meet up with Shipton.

On October 3, 1982, Dutch climber Johan Taks, a member of the Dutch Everest expedition, climbed Changtse without a permit and against the wishes of his expedition leader. Contemporary Dutch accounts described him setting out alone after being ordered not to, returning later that day to announce success.

Changtse from the upper slopes of Lhakpa Ri. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

Eleven days after Taks’ unauthorized solo push, on October 14, 1982, the first official ascent of Changtse was achieved by members of a German party.

The German Alpine Club team, co-led by Eduard Geyer and Hansjuergen Tauscher, approached the mountain via the East Rongbuk route. The expedition included climbers Paul Braun, Thomas Dunsser, Martin Engler, Walter Ernst, Rudolf Frick, Andreas Heckmair Jr., Ludwig Hoesle, Peter Lechart, Udo Zehetleitner, and Wilfried Zink.

The team drove from Lhasa and established their Base Camp near the final moraine of the Rongbuk Glacier at 5,105m. From there, they pushed up Everest and Changtse without the help of high-altitude porters. The climbers relied on their own strength and a team of six yaks to establish Camp 1 at 5,601m on October 2, followed two days later by Camp 2 at 6,096m, at the foot of Changtse’s long northeast ridge.

To get higher, the climbers first had to climb a difficult 610m snow-and-ice slope mixed with exposed rock. They established Camp 3 at 6,400m, sheltered behind a protective rock spur. Above this point, they fixed ropes along a steep slope on a wide ridge that curved first north and then sloped east. On October 13, they successfully placed Camp 4 high on the ridge at 6,903m.

On October 14, Zehetleitner completed the first official ascent, climbing via the four-kilometer northeast ridge, starting from the junction of the East Rongbuk and Changtse Glaciers. Two days later, on October 16, Braun, Frick, Hoesle, and Engler also topped out. They listed Changtse’s height as 7,550m.

Everest and Changtse. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

In May 1983, the first Chilean expedition to Everest was already stretched thin by high altitude and extreme logistics when internal friction pushed the team over the edge. Among the climbers was 25-year-old glaciologist Gino Casassa, who had been temporarily sidelined by altitude sickness and was sent down to Base Camp to recover.

As his health improved, Casassa grew restless under the strict commands of his expedition leader, Gaston Oyarzun. Forbidden from taking unnecessary risks, Casassa instead fixed his sights on Changtse. At 3:30 am on May 14, Casassa secretly slipped out of camp alone, starting an unauthorized solo attempt up the mountain’s long northeast ridge — the same route used by the Germans.

Moving rapidly in the subzero darkness without a permit, radio communication, or backup, he gambled everything on a lightweight style. By 3:30 pm, he was just 10m below the summit. However, the upper sections of the ridge deteriorated into unstable snow cornices and deep powder. Casassa narrowly escaped disaster when the snowpack fractured and slumped 4.5m beneath his boots, threatening to trigger a massive avalanche down the face.

Refusing to retreat, Casassa bypassed the unstable ridge by traversing directly onto the steep, exposed north face. He finally reached the summit at 5:00 pm. After a difficult descent in the dark, he reached Camp 2 at 11:00 pm, exhausted and dehydrated.

Back at camp, his unexpected return sparked outrage rather than celebration. While Casassa was on the peak, his teammates were managing a high-altitude medical emergency, and his unauthorized disappearance had caused immense panic.

Because the climb lacked official Chinese permits, it also carried diplomatic risks for future Chilean expeditions. The Chilean Mountaineering Federation officially expelled Casassa, concluding one of the era’s most astonishing solo feats with immediate controversy.

In May 1986, a massive Chinese–Japanese expedition (17 Japanese and 19 Chinese climbers) targeted the mountain. After establishing an Advance Base at the confluence of the Changtse and East Rongbuk Glaciers, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier and the northeast ridge.

On May 10, 16 climbers reached the summit. Among them was Tibetan climber Gunsang (also spelled Guisang), who became the first woman to summit Changtse. A second wave of eight Chinese climbers topped out the following day, while the remaining Japanese climbers withdrew to assist a teammate suffering from high-altitude sickness. According to the Himalayan Database, Gunsang remains the only woman to summit.

Ed Webster’s photo on August 26, 1986, during his first attempt on Changtse’s Northeast Ridge. Two days later, he established a new route, solo via the Southeast Face. Photo: Ed Webster

Later that same summer, American mountaineer Ed Webster arrived to attempt a bold, lightweight climb.

On August 26, 1986, he initially turned back from 7,163m on the right side of the face because of dangerously thin snow over brittle shale. After just a single rest day, he launched another attempt on August 28 and established a landmark new route up the southeast face.

Starting from an Advance Base at 6,126m near the foot of the North Col, Webster climbed the lower, highly avalanche-prone sections in total darkness to capitalize on the stable nighttime freeze. He navigated a prominent snow gully between two massive rock buttresses, traversed the upper face, and connected with the German northeast ridge route to reach the summit alone in a 15-hour round trip.

In September 1987, an Australian expedition led by Robert Turner arrived at the East Rongbuk side of the mountain. On September 29, despite punishing high-altitude winds and deteriorating conditions, Turner and Glen Nash reached the summit. They climbed via a central couloir to the left of the north face icefall. This completed a line that was closely related to a route scouted by a Japanese team the previous year.

Changtse attracted global attention in late summer 2016 because of two remarkable solo ascents. Jordi Tosas of Spain reached the summit via the east ridge on August 27, and Kilian Jornet followed on September 11, via a variant line up the northeast face.

The total number of Changtse summits remains low, at around 60. The standard line remains the northeast ridge.

Illustrated photo of the 2016 expedition for the American Alpine Journal. From the approach to the north: (A) Point 6,822m; (B) Everest; and (C) Changtse. (1) Approach to the east ridge of Changtse (first ascent 1982). (2) Jornet variant on the north face (2016). (3) Japanese variant on the north face (1986). Photo: Jordi Tosas

#8408. Everest Climbers Return to West Ridge With One Member Less

On their second venture up Everest, the Russian team is aiming to progress further along the West Ridge. This time, they will be a team of just three: Natalya Belyankina was airlifted out yesterday due to health problems.

Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will climb one of the longest routes of Everest, with no supplemental oxygen, no support team, and no clear idea about the exact line they will follow.

Kondrashkin recently posted details about their previous ascent to the Lho La and the beginning of the ridge last week. As he noted, their route skirts below gigantic hanging seracs. They felt safe traversing the area on the way up because they saw no avalanche debris. However, after they reached the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide col, the boom of a falling serac below them reminded them of the risks.

On the following morning, the climbers approached the first part of the West Ridge.

“[It was] a sharp ascent to the ridge: first, on a 50˚ snow slope and, higher up, more than 100m of 60˚ glacial ice,” Kondrashkin recalled. “Then, climbing over a slight snow cornice, we emerged onto the ridge.”

Shipilov and Vasiliev climbed further up a rocky outcrop, looking for both the most suitable line and a potential campsite on the ridge. They also photographed the sections ahead. As Kondrashkin and Belyankina watched from below, “It felt like we were looking at it from the very foot of the mountain, just how enormous it is,” Kondrashkin wrote about Everest’s upper half:

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Serguey Kondrashkin

The team returned to Base Camp the following day, finding a better route that involves less time under the hanging seracs.

Since then, they have been resting and preparing for the next foray up. However, the rest was not enough for Natalya Belyankina, who was already suffering from a bad case of Khumbu cough.

Natalya Belyankina in the helicopter back to Kathmandu today. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

“It’s a real pity,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote today. “Natasha did so much to make this expedition happen, but it’s impossible to continue in this condition.”

Vasiliev then confirmed that Kondrashkin, Shipilov, and he are heading up again today for about a week.

The Russians are the only climbers currently on an 8,000m peak, and their goal is among the most ambitious on Everest in years. They intend to climb the mountain entirely on their own, without supplemental oxygen, in a light style, via the West Ridge.

On Pete Poston’s graph of Everest routes, the Yugoslavian route is #5 in pink, and the 1963 U.S. route is #2 in green.

The West Ridge of Everest has been climbed just three times, each via different variations, all of them epic and sometimes tragic expeditions. Climbing the West Ridge involves two possible routes. First, an endless climb along the ridge from Nepal like the 1979 Yugoslavian team did (Andrej Stremfelj, Nejc Zaplotnik, Stipe Bozic, Stane Belak-Srauf, and Ang Phu Sherpa).

Second, they could cross into Tibet at some point and continue up the North Face via the Hornbein Couloir. This route retraces the steps of Americans Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, who started up the normal route to Camp 2, then joined the West Ridge and crossed to what became known as the Hornbein Couloir to the summit in 1963.

#8407. Xpedition NexLite 35 Bow Review: Accuracy and Speed Test

Published Oct 29, 2026 1:00 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Late October is a great time to be a bowhunter. The bucks are chasing, and new bows seem to drop every week. One of them recently showed up on my front porch. (I’m still working on getting a buck to do that.) This one is a 35-inch featherweight from Xpedition, and on paper, its long axle-to-axle length and low mass weight make it a strong pick for anyone who wants one bow for both targets and the whitetail woods. I spent the last two weeks shooting the new Xpedition Nexlite 35 to find out if it lives up to that promise.

A typical 35-inch bow weighs 4.6 to 4.9 pounds. The NexLite 35 weighs 3.95 pounds. That weight savings comes from the Magnite riser material, which is a nanocomposite alloy that’s about 30 percent lighter than 6061 aluminum. Xpedition says it’s also stronger and absorbs vibration better than aluminum and carbon.

Low-profile arrow rest and sight mounting are now standard on premium and even budget compound bows. You’ll find Integrate rest mounting and a machined Picatinny sight mount on the NexLite 35. Xpedition also offers its XLOK accessories, such as a low-profile quiver and a bow stand.

The NexLite 35 uses the Tip-Shift tuning system. It’s a simple shimming system that doesn’t require a bow press. All you need is an Allen wrench to swap the shims and move your cams.

Before I fired my first shot from the NexLite 35, I was impressed with how light it is for a 35-inch bow. It’s only 4.9 pounds fully rigged with an XLOK stabilizer, Axcel Armortech sight, XLOK bow stand, and QAD arrow rest. Its low mass weight gives you the flexibility to run it as a lightweight hunting bow or rig it with long stabilizers for TAC and 3D competitions.

I paper tuned the NexLite without any drama. I didn’t need to use the Tip-Shift tuning system, but I did use it during the 2026 bow test. It’s a fantastically simple system. All you need to do is remove a screw with an Allen wrench and replace the spacer with the one that will fix your issue. The spacers have one, two, or three dots on them. The number of dots you install should always add up to four. I like that the Tip-Shift is a rigid system, so you don’t run the risk of an adjustment screw walking or accidentally moving a cam too far.

The NexLite 35’s draw cycle is smooth, but you can tell the cams were built for speed. The bow hits its peak weight early, evens out, and then there’s a final effort right before the valley. To me, it feels similar to drawing a Mathews Lift. The wall is solid with no give, and the valley is relatively short. If you come off the stops, the bow will let you know you’re creeping. But I found it very easy to keep the stops pinned, and the bow felt exceptionally comfortable and stable at full draw. It’s easy to drop the pin on the target and keep it there. At the shot, there is minimal vibration, which is impressive considering the bow’s low weight.

I quickly got used to the draw cycle while sighting in. Then I stepped back to 50 yards for accuracy testing and —— buddy, this bow is a shooter. I shot five five-shot groups at 50 yards that averaged 3.19 inches.

For the speed test, I shot a 430-grain arrow with the bow set at 61.2 pounds and a 31.5-inch draw length. The four-shot average was 281.6 fps. That’s pretty fast for a 35-inch bow.

The NexLite has nearly all the features you’d expect in a modern flagship bow, but there are three features I’d like to see added.

If you’re in the market for a long axle-to-axle bow, the NexLite 35 is definitely worth trying out at your local shop. It’s a top contender because its low mass weight makes it versatile as a combination target and hunting bow. It also has good performance, an easy-to-use tuning system, and high accuracy potential. I also really appreciate the NexLite 35’s build quality. It’s beautifully finished and masterfully machined — the type of workmanship I love to see in a premium bow.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8406. Alaska to Patagonia, One Summit at a Time

Since 1972, Alaska to Patagonia has been a classic cycling route of 30,000km or more. At any given time, several ambitious cyclists are attempting it. But no one is doing it quite like Tobias Renggli of Lucerne, Switzerland.

The 23-year-old endurance athlete is not only pedaling the distance but also climbing the highest peak in each of the 35 countries he passes through. And although it’s part of the marketing rather than the adventure, the imagery so far — shot both by Renggli and by a film production group he belongs to called the Black Forest Collective — is stunning for such a difficult journey.

Despite his age, this is not Renggli’s first adventure. In 2022, at the age of 18, he cycled all 44 European countries within seven months, climbing the highest peak of each and camping every night. In 2024, he climbed the highest mountains of all 26 Swiss cantons in about three weeks.

Renggli began in April from Deadhorse, Alaska, on the shores of the Beaufort Sea — still deep winter at that latitude, though the long Arctic days had returned. Pedaling 1,200km in temperatures as low as -30˚C, he made his way to Talkeetna, then skied in for eight days while pulling a sled.

He then summited 6,190m McKinley with his occasional partner, Heli Hofmann — the first party atop the peak this year, which meant they had to break trail through the deep snow. It took them 36 days.

Next, it was onto 5,959m Mount Logan, Canada’s highest peak. Again with Heli Hofmann but no guide, they summited in late June. This time, they were the last party of the year to summit Logan.

Renggli then cycled with another friend to Vancouver, took a two-week break after covering 3,000km and summiting two of the hardest peaks he would encounter, then continued alone through the U.S. Typically, he cycles 100 to 160km per day, with some shorter days.

Unlike most Trans-America cyclists, he chose to take Baja California rather than mainland Mexico. Crossing Baja was more difficult than expected. He described temperatures exceeding 40°C and a 120km stretch toward Loreto that he began with only two liters of water.

Later, near Ciudad Insurgentes, thunderstorms flooded the roads. At night, he carried his bicycle through a fast-moving, thigh-deep flood while vehicles turned back.

Renggli had intended to take no motorized transportation, only sailboats when confronted with water — he also wants to climb 12 high points in the Caribbean. However, this is such a massive undertaking that he’s not being too strict on himself. Although he skied into Denali, for example, he flew back out to Talkeetna. And from La Paz in Baja, he caught the ferry to Mazatlan on the mainland and continued from there.

Details have been sparse since Baja, but Renggli recently crossed into Guatemala. Presumably, he climbed 5,636m Pico de Orizaba before leaving Mexico and is now headed to 4,220m Volcán Tajumulco, Guatemala’s highest peak. He has been on the road for 202 days.

#8405. The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

As every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

So I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

As the midterm elections showed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

As long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

But that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The new car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

If you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

If you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

Retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

How do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:

So how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

According to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market shows up about once every six years.

In other words, if you plan on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

Hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

But here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

My takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, plan on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

During a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

During a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, new socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

With this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

You can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

The market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

If your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your plan has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

#8404. Australian Grandfather Attempts 1,650Km River Swim

Australian grain farm manager Scott Gladman, 63, is attempting to swim the length of the Darling River, Australia’s third-longest river. It begins in New South Wales and finishes at its confluence with the Murray River at Wentworth. Gladman believes he will be the first person to swim the entire 1,650km route.

Gladman started on September 1 from near Brewarrina in far north New South Wales. At the outset, he budgeted 103 days to complete the swim, averaging around 16km per day. So far, he is largely on track. After 49 days, he has covered 660km, leaving just under 1,000km to go.

Interestingly, the expedition is not born from a love of endurance swimming. Gladman was inspired to find a fundraising challenge to support friends impacted by Motor Neuron Disease and Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, a rare form of Parkinson’s. Initially, he considered the Murray. “I just thought I could swim the Murray River, but people have done that,” he told ABC News. “No one has had a crack at the Darling.”

The location of the Darling River in Australia. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Gladman gave himself 18 months to train. In the summer, he swam in the Murray River at Boundary Bend, Victoria, and during winter he completed laps in indoor pools. Now out on the Darling, a support boat of family and friends keeps him company, alongside a canoeist.

“There’s no real form of communication, and I wear earplugs…he’ll [the canoeist] either have to hit me on the back of the head with a paddle to get my attention, or he’ll just start steering toward me, and that will push me one way or the other,” Gladman said.

Despite its length, the Darling River is sometimes so shallow that Gladman needs to float through sections on his back, or walk. The support boat also sometimes requires saving, with Gladman having to help clear a path through river debris:

#8401. The Biggest Archery Mistakes You’re Making This Bow Season

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:22 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Over the past 20 years, I’ve shot, competed with and hunted with everything from selfbows to compounds. If there’s a mistake you can make while shooting a bow, I’ve done it. Luckily, I’ve also had the chance to learn from world-class coaches, Olympians, and the best archers in the world. So I’ve learned how to fix the worst errors and spot trouble in other bowhunters.

Here are five common archery mistakes that new and experienced bowhunters make that ultimately cost opportunities in the field.

The easiest archery flaw to fix is also one of the most common ones. When you grip your bow properly, it becomes easier to tune, and your accuracy will improve because you won’t induce inconsistent torque into the bow. To grip your bow, place your hand as high as it will go in the grip, turn your knuckles so they’re at a 45-degree angle to the riser and make sure the bow touches your hand only between your thumb pad and lifeline.

Read Next: How to Grip a Compound Bow for Better Hunting Accuracy

Have you ever used the wrong pin, forgotten to look through your peep or fired as soon as your pin was close to a deer’s kill zone? Those mistakes happen because you’re relying on your subconscious to shoot the bow.

In the backyard, you can let your subconscious run the shot. Heck, you could shoot half asleep and do all right. But shooting under pressure is a different story. You can’t trust your subconscious in those situations because it will take shortcuts to skip to the ultimate goal — firing the arrow. It’s a lot like AI: It finds the most efficient solution, and wiping you out might be mere collateral damage.

Instead of relying on autopilot, you need a firm shot process that you fully control. Make a list of the key steps of your shot and check them off one by one. This keeps you in the present and focused on the process, not the result.

Read Next: Target Panic! Joel Turner and Joe Rogan Talk Archery

With time and repetitions, your strings can move, which affects your bow’s tune and sight tape. Don’t be one of those hunters who misses an easy shot because their sight was off or their drop-away rest timing changed. Every month or so, check your sight and rest timing, shoot your bow through paper and make sure your broadheads are in tune.

When you first learned to shoot a bow, someone probably told you that you need a consistent anchor point. But that doesn’t mean you need to anchor the string into your face. Pressing your face or your nose against the string causes oscillation, which leads to left-and-right inconsistencies. The string can touch your face, but only lightly.

If you find yourself trying really hard to hold your bow steady, you’re approaching archery the wrong way. A steady aim is the result of your form and bow setup. There’s no muscling your way to it. You also can’t make your pin stop moving. The goal is for your pin to have a slow, consistent float around the spot. Once you achieve that, your next job is to focus on shot execution.

When you make a change to your archery form or your bow, it’s normal for your accuracy to suffer at first. Trust the process during that learning period, and shoot at a big target such as the Blackout Longshot 36. The goal during the period is to get used to your change and not care about accuracy until your shot feels good again.

#8399. Seven Alpine-Style Climbs Happening Now in Nepal

Several small teams are attempting difficult climbs on Nepal’s 6,000 and 7,000m peaks. Unfortunately, they rarely report on their plans or progress until they return, and often only if they succeed.

This is what we know about the ongoing expeditions:

Three young French climbers, members of the Military High Mountain Group from Chamonix, celebrated their organization’s 50th anniversary with a new route on Peak 41. This 6,654m mountain is located in the Khumbu region and is often called the “true Mera Peak.”

Konrad Piontek, Amaury Fouillade, and Clovis Paulin took advantage of a good weather window and achieved the first ascent of the peak’s northeast face. They climbed in an alpine-style single push over four days. The result is a beautiful 1,400m line with difficulties up to ED+ 5+ M6 A1 90°. They descended via the southeast face. The team named their line Bon Matin (good morning).

Nivel Meroi and Romano Benet are acclimatized and ready to attempt a new route on Jugal II, but the Italian couple will be on their own. Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, has left due to illness.

Meanwhile, in the Kangchenjunga region, a large Russian team has also finished acclimatizing. The team trekked in the area and crossed a number of high-altitude passes, the latest of them at the top of an icefall at 5,750m. They reported lots of snow above 5,000m but are ready to attempt a new route on the formidable Jannu (7,710m) from its southeast side.

The team comprises Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin.

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan traveled to Nepal in September, aiming to achieve the first ascent of Gangapurna West (7,455m), also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal. They have provided no news since, but they probably had to retreat when an intense snowstorm hit the Annapurna region three weeks ago.

Location of Gangapurna West on a Google Earth screenshot. Notes by Lindsay Griffin for the American Alpine Journal.

Meanwhile, a second team has reached the base of the peak with the same objective. Valery Shamalo, Natalia Zanina, Maksim Trufanov, and Ruslan Kirichenko arrived at the beginning of October and saw no one else there. They reported that recent precipitation had left the trail in a poor state; the climbers had to cross landslides and swollen rivers to reach base camp.

The team has completed two acclimatization climbs, looking for a passage through the icefall at the base of the mountain and then a series of couloirs. They reached 5,900m and, on a second trip, 6,600m. Deep snow covered the peak, which slowed progress. Finally, they launched a summit bid last week.

From 6,600m, they spent a day on technical ice sections of 70–80º. In poor visibility, they endured spindrift and were showered by small ice chunks.

“In the afternoon, the weather deteriorated sharply,” Natalia Zanina said. “Heavy snowfall began, and we started being struck by large, continuous avalanches. At 6,800m (340m from the summit), we decided to turn back.”

A note on names: according to 8000ers.com, Asapurna should be the correct name for this peak because — although it is closer to Gangapurna — Asapurna’s summit ridge connects directly to Annapurna III.

The list of climbing permits granted by Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism points to some other interesting expeditions, some of them in remote western Nepal. There is a permit for Nyalu Kang (6,265m), only opened to foreign climbers in 2024 and reportedly unclimbed, and Ardang, summited once by Canadians Bryce Kendall and Sunny Twelker in 2019. Victor Saunders and Mick Fowler of the UK attempted Ardang last year.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8397. ‘It’s Trailer Park Chemistry.’ A Hybrid Bighorn Sheep Is on the Lam and That Could Be Bad News for Wild Herds

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The two-paragraph Sept. 18 news release from Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks raised more questions than it may have intended.

The department “is seeking help from the public to locate a hybridized female rocky mountain bighorn sheep that went missing from a private alternative livestock facility near Vaughn in early September,” the release from FWP’s Region 4 office in Great Falls stated. “The bighorn ewe is described as weighing about 120 pounds and is primarily white in color with a red ear tag.”

The news release stressed wildlife officials’ concern that the ewe could come into contact with wild bighorn sheep in the vicinity. Domestic sheep are often vectors for pathogens that can fatally infect wild sheep.

What the news release didn’t disclose is that the “alternative livestock facility” in question is owned by Arthur “Jack” Schubarth, who was convicted in 2024 of violating the federal Lacey Act in his pursuit to create giant hybrid bighorn rams. Schubarth pleaded guilty to helping smuggle genetic material from Marco Polo argali sheep from Kyrgyzstan into the United States in order to clone the ram and create a “super sheep” with huge spiraling horns and resistance to the pathogens that infect North American wild sheep. His quest was enabled by Montana hunting outfitter John Lewton, who lopped off the testicles of his clients’ trophy wild bighorns, kept the gonads on ice, and later sold them to Schubarth.

The idea, Schubarth later told court officials, was to use the genetic material to incubate hybrid sheep with horns larger than any North American rams.

Lewton was sentenced last week in federal court in Billings and received a $20,000 fine and a year of probation for his part in the genetic alchemy. As a condition of his federal-court sentence, Lewton is prohibited from outfitting or guiding hunters for a full year.

The notion that a “Frankenram” could be produced with a combination of cloned embryos and artificial insemination isn’t an abstraction. In 2017, Schubarth actually produced what he called the Montana Mountain King, a pure cloned Marco Polo ram birthed to a surrogate bighorn ewe. Schubarth subsequently bred offspring of the Montana Mountain King to captive bighorn ewes on his farm west of Great Falls. It’s one of these ewes that has now gone missing, according to Fish, Wildlife & Parks.

Schubarth’s genetic hermetics has both baffled and impressed wildlife investigators, who told Outdoor Life that the sort of reproductive science that Schubarth practiced is normally limited to hospitals, universities, and other science centers with state-of-the-art facilities.

“The best way to describe his operation is trailer-park chemistry,” said a source familiar with the case who spoke on background. “He’s pulled off a pretty high-level genetics program with hardware-store gear and limited resources.”

Schubarth received probation for his guilty plea to the Lacey Act violations. In his petition to the federal court for leniency, Schubarth’s attorney, Jason Holden, noted his client’s contribution to the science of wildlife propagation.

“Jack is an 81-year-old non-violent man,” Holden wrote in 2024. “His crime, the cloning of a Marco Polo Sheep from Kyrgyzstan, has ruined his life, reputation and family. Jack did something no one else could, or has ever done. On a ranch, in a barn in Montana, he created Montana Mountain King. MMK is an extraordinary animal, born of science, and from a man who, if he could rewrite history, would have left the challenge of cloning a Marco Polo to only the imagination of Michael Crichton.”

Read Next: Montana Man Charged for Illegally Cloning and Breeding Marco Polo Sheep from Central Asia

The department’s all-points-bulletin asking the public to report a lone and roaming ewe may not produce any sightings. That’s because there’s a possibility that the ewe isn’t actually on the lam. She may have been sold to an out-of-state game farm, said sources who spoke to Outdoor Life on the condition that they wouldn’t be identified based on the speculative nature of their hunches.

Schubarth, who is on probation from the 2024 federal wildlife-trafficking charges, has been charged by FWP with failure to report the escape of an animal permitted in his commercial wildlife operation, according to charging documents at the Cascade County District Court in Montana.

The “game farm” permit requires that if anything escapes the permitted facility, owners must report within 48 hours to both FWP and the Montana Department of Livestock.

“According to our records, the ewe in question reportedly escaped on Sept. 2, and our game wardens heard about it the next week,” says Dave Hagengruber, FWP’s public information officer in the Great Falls regional office. “Wardens went out to talk with Schubarth in mid-September, and he basically said, ‘Oh yeah, I meant to tell you.’”

Schubarth told wardens the ewe likely escaped either over a fence damaged by a wind storm or through a gate accidentally left open at the end of his property, beyond lines of kennels of dogs that produce puppies sold in Schubarth’s pet store in Great Falls.

Assuming the ewe did leave Schubarth’s facility, it could pose a risk to the region’s wild sheep.

“Cascade is 30 miles from his farm, and there’s a sizeable band of [wild] bighorns there,” says Hagengruber. “The Birdtail Hills are 20 to 25 miles to the west, and there are bighorns in those hills. The Rocky Mountain Front, home to Montana’s most treasured bighorn sheep herd, is 60 or 70 miles west. Fortunately, this is not a ram, so it’s less likely to roam widely, but the threat of disease transmission is a significant concern. That’s why we want to hear of any sightings. It’s Jack’s property and his responsibility to locate and return to his facility, but we can’t have this hybrid sheep potentially contacting wild bands.”

Schubarth insists he did not sell the ewe, and suspects the fugitive sheep was killed by predators within a few miles of his facility in the Sun River Valley.

“I haven’t heard anything about her, and to my knowledge Fish and Game hasn’t heard anything for five weeks now,” Schubarth said in an interview. “With all the people out looking, we haven’t seen it and no one’s called me. I’m assuming, with her lack of experience with predators, that a coyote got her.”

“She’s mainly bighorn and probably three or four domestic crosses from the original cross that was 50 percent bighorn,” Schubarth said. “I added some more bighorn from that original [parentage]. So they’re probably 62.5 percent bighorn. They don’t have any experience of being wild. I’m pretty sure she would have watched coyotes walk right up to her” without trying to evade them.

Schubarth further confirmed that he still has “around 45 head of sheep, is all” remaining on his 200-acre game farm. “All my sheep are sold right now and just waiting to leave. I’ve kept them back because I just want the pleasure of birthing out the lambs. It’s something I like to do, and at 83 years old, I like to see new life.”

As for the descendants of the Montana Mountain King, Schubarth said that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service required him to destroy progeny of the cloned ram back in 2024. The federal court also required Schubarth to dispose of all hybrid bighorn sheep by Dec. 31, 2025, and to stop “from engaging in breeding activity of big game stock while on supervision,” according to sentencing documents.

“We had 190 head of the hybrid Marco/bighorn here at the ranch and none of them got pneumonia in the three years I held them while waiting for a forever home for them. All were slaughtered,” he says. “I did sell some, 15 in all. There are some down in Texas, and every so often I see on Facebook somebody advertising a Marco Polo, but there’s no way they are more than about a quarter Marco” based on genetic dilution, he said.

As for the Montana Mountain King himself, Schubarth says the ram ended up at a zoological park in upstate New York. Indeed, last summer the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, announced the acquisition of “Tilek,” the cloned argali at the center of Schubarth’s case. The ram had been held at an Oregon wildlife rehabilitation center for over three years before being moved to the Syracuse zoo.

Schubarth says “Tilek” would be about nine years old, but observed that he has not yet expressed the most distinctive trait of the Marco Polo subspecies of argali: its spiraling horns.

“He’s basically still 54 to 57 inches,” says Schubarth. “He ought to have 75 inches of horn on each side. But this year they put him in a larger grass pen so maybe he’ll grow more. For safety’s sake, they should have castrated him so no more genetics could get out there. Maybe they did, for all I know. I’ll never see him again. I don’t ever leave my ranch.”

Schubarth said that statements from prosecutors that he was motivated to create a hybrid ram with giant horns in order to upsell to commercial shooting operations are wrong. He was more interested in cross-breeding to create a bighorn race that might be resistant to what’s often called “M. ovi,” a respiratory disease that often results in catastrophic pneumonia-caused die-offs in wild sheep.

“My thinking was that here’s this wild sheep that has evolved with domestic sheep for thousands of years,” says Schubarth of the Marco Polo, native to the high alpine plateaus of central Asia. “The feds and Fish and Game made it out that I was selling to the hunt community and only motivated to create bigger horns. In actuality, I was after the immune system, and the reality is that even after several generations, these Marco hybrids still seem to be immune to pneumonia. I think that’s the real story.”

If he regrets anything about the misadventures of the Montana Mountain King, it’s that he trusted the lab that created the clone from genetic tissue smuggled from Kyrgyzstan.

“I’ve been happy all my life except for this last foolishness about the Marco Polo,” Schubarth says. “I wouldn’t have done it had the cloning company not told me it was legal. They lied after they took $32,000 from me. That was the cost of stockpiling the tissue and making the embryos for me.”

The rest of the genetic work was a cinch, he says. The surrogate bighorn ewes, most of which Schubarth bought from zoos in Canada and Colorado, were selected for their ability to carry the hybrid lamb.

“Laparoscopic work is easy,” he says, and artificial insemination is an established livestock practice. The trick is creating a genetically manipulated zygote.

“You take the egg and suck out the product and you put the material from the Marco Polo into the egg and implant it in a ewe. A little electricity, and poof, the thing starts to grow.”

Schubarth says he will be entirely out of the game-breeding business by 2027.

“Fish and Game has accomplished what they always wanted: to drive me out of business,” he says.

Meanwhile, he says the captive-shooting industry is thriving. He cites high-fence operations in Kansas and Texas that would pay top dollar for his hybrid bighorns while also insisting that he sold to fellow breeders, not trophy hunters.

“The feds made it out that I was the center of this industry based on shooting animals in pens,” he says, before acknowledging that most of his animals probably met that fate. “Without the interest of the hunting community, these animals would be worthless and only sold for meat. So yes, the industry revolves around the harvesting of these animals by collectors.”

Fish, Wildlife & Parks is less interested in the commercial than in the pathological outcome of the case. The state has struggled to establish bighorn sheep populations in prime habitat in the Missouri River Breaks and in the mountains of southwest Montana. Bands that thrive for years are often wiped out in a single season by pneumonia epizootics that often originate in domestic sheep.

State game wardens are authorized to shoot on sight wild bighorns that contact domestic sheep. The fear is that a traveling ram could become infected by a domestic sheep, and then take that pathogen back to the wild herd.

“We have spent many years and sportsmen’s dollars to restore and transplant wild sheep into available habitat in Montana,” says FWP’s Hagengruber. “We’ve had recent restorations in the Belts and the Breaks, and disease is always a big concern, and so is the ability of this hybrid ewe to breed with either domestic or wild sheep. So we take the possibility that there may be a hybrid domestic/wild sheep running around central Montana very seriously.”

Anyone who sees a lone sheep with a red ear tag in central Montana is urged to call FWP’s Region 4 office at 406-454-5840.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.
